title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk

paper.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
paper.abstract:
Abstract Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined. Keywords: calibration, hidden Markov model, income risk,
likelihood, misspecification, precautionary saving. JEL codes: C13, C52, C63, D15, E21.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Quantitative macroeconomics often disciplines models by calibration. A researcher chooses parameters so that the model reproduces a small set of selected moments of the data, and then uses the model to study behavior, welfare, or policy ( Kydland & Prescott, 1982c ; Kydland & Prescott, 1996c ) . 1 1 1 We use “calibration” to include procedures that fit a small set of selected moments, including the simulated method of moments as used in our application. Calibration is transparent and directs attention to features that the researcher considers important. However, agreement with the targets is evidence only about the targets. Different models, or different parameters within one model, may reproduce the same targets and still imply different responses to risk and policy ( Hansen & Heckman, 1996c ; Browning et al., 1999c ) . Whether this concern matters in practice is an empirical question: does matching the targets pin down the economic answer? Answering this question requires a criterion that uses more information than the selected moments. The likelihood is such a criterion. It evaluates the joint distribution of complete observed histories, so a model can reproduce selected statistics and still assign low probability to the histories from which we compute those statistics. The obstacle is computation. When a model contains a latent (unobserved) state with nonlinear dynamics or non-Gaussian shocks, the Kalman filter no longer applies, and the likelihood requires integrating over all possible paths of the latent state. Particle filters approximate this integral by simulation ( Fernández-Villaverde & Rubio-Ramírez, 2007c ) , but the simulated likelihood contains sampling noise and is not smooth in the parameters, which complicates optimization. For these reasons, likelihood comparison remains rare in quantitative work. In this paper, we show that maximum likelihood estimation of nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent-state models on short, irregular panels is now feasible, and that it leads to economic answers different from those of calibration. In our application, calibrations of a single earnings model fit the targets about equally well, yet imply mean assets that differ by a factor of about three, with the same data, preferences, and prices. The likelihood, by contrast, ranks the models and their parameters by their fit to complete earnings histories. We approximate the continuous latent state by a finite-state Markov chain while leaving the observations continuous. This approximation turns the model into a hidden Markov model (HMM), in which an unobserved finite-state chain generates the observed outcomes ( Kitagawa, 1987c ; Farmer, 2021g ) . For discrete-time processes, we construct the chain by the conditional moment matching method of Farmer & Toda (2017g) . For a diffusion, we discretize its generator (the operator that describes the local drift and variance of the diffusion). The HMM forward recursion sums over all latent histories by successive matrix multiplications. We integrate permanent individual effects (time-invariant unobserved differences) by numerical quadrature. We retain each individual’s entry age and use transition matrices for the actual observation gaps, so irregular observation dates pose no difficulty. The likelihood requires no simulation, and standard optimizers estimate all parameters jointly. We also provide a framework for inference and model comparison under misspecification. We treat each complete history as one independent observation and let the number of individuals grow while histories remain short. Under stated identification and regularity conditions, we give inference for the parameters and compare non-nested models using individual log likelihood differences ( White, 1982c ; Vuong, 1989c ) . The population likelihood ranks models by their Kullback–Leibler divergence (a measure of the discrepancy between two probability distributions) from the data distribution. We distinguish inference for the fixed finite-state approximation from inference for the continuous-state model, and we state conditions on the numerical approximation error. We apply the HMM approach to earnings dynamics, a central input into quantitative household models. We use 28,422 biennial observations of 4,683 men aged 30–60 from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), after removing deterministic earnings effects. We compare four processes for the persistent component of earnings. Our benchmark is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process, which is a Gaussian AR(1) at annual dates. The second is a stationary adaptation of Guvenen, Karahan, Ozkan & Song (2021g) (GKOS), an AR(1) whose innovations are a mixture of Gaussian distributions. The third is a stationary adaptation of Guvenen, McKay & Ryan (2026g) (GMR), an AR(1) with losses that affect both current earnings and the persistent state. The fourth is our piecewise linear variance (PLV) diffusion, whose volatility depends on the persistent state. Each process also includes permanent individual effects and either Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks, giving eight specifications. We show that all four stationary processes can share the entire earnings covariance function (Proposition 4.1 ). Thus second moments alone cannot separate them. Our application leads to three main results. First, the likelihood distinguishes the candidate specifications. Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks improve the log likelihood by more than 1,500 points in every model. Under this specification, PLV has the highest likelihood, followed by GKOS, GMR, and OU. The data favor PLV and GKOS over GMR but do not clearly separate PLV from GKOS. Second, close target fit need not extend to complete earnings histories. We calibrate each process with mixture transitory shocks to 70 moments of earnings changes and levels, following the designs of Guvenen et al. (2021g) ; Guvenen et al. (2026g) as closely as our data allow. To prevent cherry-picking, we fixed the targets and weights before computing any results. The calibrations match the percentiles of changes and levels closely and lower the moment objective by about 80 percent relative to the likelihood estimates. Yet all four calibrations fit the histories worse than every likelihood-estimated specification with mixture transitory shocks, including OU. 2 2 2 An earlier calibration to 18 moments of earnings changes only, in which GKOS and GMR match the targets within our tolerance, leads to the same conclusions (Appendix D.7 ). Third, the empirical criterion changes both the level of saving and the ranking of models. We solve a standard optimal saving problem, holding preferences, prices, mean earnings, and transfers fixed. When we match the processes to the fitted OU covariance function, PLV moves from the most wealth to the least, and mean assets fall within 4.2 to 4.8, compared with 4.8 to 10.5 under likelihood estimation. Calibrated PLV implies mean assets of 3.76, compared with 10.51 under likelihood estimation. Among evaluated calibrations whose objectives lie within 0.0092 of the reported objective, mean assets range from 2.2 to 8.2 for GKOS and from 3.1 to 9.3 for PLV. Thus close target fit can leave the economic answer largely undetermined. These results do not mean that the likelihood-preferred model is correct. Every model we consider is misspecified, and the fitted models still miss features of the data, including the extreme kurtosis of earnings changes. We therefore recommend a division of labor: use the likelihood to compare and select models, and use targeted moments to diagnose where the selected model fails. The HMM approach applies whenever the latent state is low-dimensional, so researchers can assess the fit of observed histories before using a model for economic analysis. In empirical industrial organization, researchers routinely estimate and test structural models by likelihood ( Rust, 1987c ) . The HMM approach makes the same discipline available for the household models of quantitative macroeconomics.

sections.heading: 1.1 Related literature
sections.text: Our paper contributes to the literature on the empirical foundations of quantitative models. Kydland & Prescott (1982c) ; Kydland & Prescott (1996c) develop and defend calibration as a computational experiment. Hansen & Heckman (1996c) and Browning et al. (1999c) examine the empirical support for the parameters and specifications used in quantitative macroeconomics. Gregory & Smith (1991c) and Canova (1994c) develop simulation-based inference for calibrated models, and Watson (1993c) measures discrepancies in their dynamic second moments. Hnatkovska et al. (2012c) compare misspecified calibrated models by minimum distance and study the role of the weighting matrix. Andrews et al. (2017c) measure the local sensitivity of parameter estimates to estimation moments. Closely related to our application, Crawley et al. (2026c) show that misspecification makes income-risk estimates depend on the moments and weights used, and they propose a richer transitory component. We instead compare models by the likelihood of complete observed histories and show that close target fit can leave economic predictions undetermined. The HMM approximation of continuous-state models has a long history. Kitagawa (1987c) evaluates non-Gaussian state-space likelihoods by numerical integration, and Langrock et al. (2012c) maximize the likelihood of fine-grid HMM approximations to nonlinear models. Farmer (2021g) develops the “discretization filter” for economic models, combines HMM likelihood evaluation with moment-matching discretizations such as Farmer & Toda (2017g) , and establishes likelihood theory for long time series. Altman (2007c) develops mixed HMMs with random effects, and Delattre et al. (2013c) study likelihood estimation of diffusions with random effects. We bring HMM likelihood evaluation and comparison into a short-panel framework with permanent heterogeneity, nonstationary initialization, and irregular observation gaps. We give inference under misspecification and separate the statistical conditions from the conditions on numerical accuracy. Our illustration builds on the earnings-dynamics literature. Abowd & Card (1989c) and Meghir & Pistaferri (2011c) study the covariance structure of earnings, and Storesletten et al. (2004c) use earnings risk in a quantitative household model. Geweke & Keane (2000c) estimate PSID earnings dynamics with normal-mixture shocks by Bayesian methods. Meghir & Pistaferri (2004c) and Botosaru & Sasaki (2018c) allow state-dependent variances, and Arellano et al. (2017c) allow nonlinear persistence. Guvenen et al. (2021g) document non-Gaussian earnings changes in administrative data, and Guvenen et al. (2026g) propose a tractable process with large losses and scarring. De et al. (2020c) and Guvenen et al. (2024c) study the consumption and welfare implications of richer earnings risk. We use earnings dynamics to demonstrate HMM model selection and measure how the choice of empirical criterion changes economic predictions.

sections.heading: 2 Hidden Markov likelihood for short panels
sections.text: In this section, we describe how we evaluate and compare likelihoods of short-panel models. We approximate the continuous latent state by a finite-state Markov chain, which turns the model into a hidden Markov model (HMM). We let the number of independent individuals grow while individual histories remain bounded in length. Our inference accommodates permanent heterogeneity without requiring the latent process to mix over time. We present the practical steps here and collect the asymptotic theory in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 2.5 Comparing misspecified models
sections.text: Our main use of the likelihood is to compare competing models that are all misspecified. Let A A and B B denote two models with population objectives 𝒬 A \mathcal{Q}^{A} and 𝒬 B \mathcal{Q}^{B} and pseudo-true values θ 0 A \theta_{0}^{A} and θ 0 B \theta_{0}^{B} , defined as in ( 2.2 ). By ( 2.4 ), the difference 𝒬 A ​ ( θ 0 A ) − 𝒬 B ​ ( θ 0 B ) \mathcal{Q}^{A}(\theta_{0}^{A})-\mathcal{Q}^{B}(\theta_{0}^{B}) equals the difference between the expected KL divergences from the actual outcome distribution to model B B and to model A A . Thus the model with the higher population objective is closer to the data in KL divergence. Under the regularity conditions of Vuong (1989c) , we use individual log likelihood differences to compare the models. Let θ ^ A \widehat{\theta}^{A} and θ ^ B \widehat{\theta}^{B} be the two estimates, and define the individual log likelihood differences d i ≔ ℓ i A ​ ( θ ^ A ) − ℓ i B ​ ( θ ^ B ) d_{i}\coloneqq\ell_{i}^{A}(\widehat{\theta}^{A})-\ell_{i}^{B}(\widehat{\theta}^{B}) , their sample mean d ¯ \bar{d} , and their sample variance σ ^ d 2 \widehat{\sigma}_{d}^{2} . When the two models are strictly non-nested and equally close to the data, the statistic I ​ d ¯ / σ ^ d \sqrt{I}\bar{d}/\widehat{\sigma}_{d} is asymptotically standard normal. Large positive values favor model A A , and large negative values favor model B B . The statistic uses only the individual log likelihoods that Algorithm 1 already computes. At a fixed grid, it compares the two discretized models. It also compares the continuous-state models when the approximation error in each total log likelihood is small relative to I ​ σ ^ d \sqrt{I}\widehat{\sigma}_{d} .

sections.heading: 3 PSID data and the Gaussian benchmark
sections.text: We illustrate likelihood-based model comparison with earnings dynamics, a central input into quantitative models of consumption, saving, and inequality. We use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) because it is widely used and readily available, allowing readers to reproduce the exercise without access to restricted administrative records. We compare models for reported earnings, which include survey noise. We describe the data and estimate a benchmark with Gaussian persistent and transitory shocks by exact maximum likelihood. We examine how permanent heterogeneity and initial dispersion affect the estimates.

sections.heading: 3.1 Data and deterministic adjustment
sections.text: We use 14 biennial PSID interviews from 1997 through 2023, which report annual labor earnings for income years 1996, 1998, …, 2022. We follow individuals using their 1968 family identifier and person number, selecting annual labor earnings for their current role as Reference Person or spouse/partner. We compute each individual’s birth year as the rounded median of interview year minus reported age. We use this birth year to define income-year age and measure elapsed time from age 30. The baseline sample contains men ages 30–60 in the income year who are current Reference Persons, spouses, or partners. We require positive, nonmissing annual labor earnings and nonmissing completed education, as well as at least two usable observations per person, but not a balanced panel. We keep only the SRC core sample (1968 family identifiers 1–2,930). This restriction drops the Census low-income oversample and the immigrant samples added from 1997, so that the unweighted sample does not overrepresent low-income households. Following Guvenen et al. (2021g) , we also require annual labor earnings of at least 13 weeks of 40 hours at half the federal minimum wage ( $ 1,885 \$1{,}885 for income years 2010–2022), which excludes observations with minimal attachment to the labor market. Table 1 reports the restrictions. The final panel contains 28,422 observations for 4,683 men. Table 1: PSID sample construction. The minimum threshold is 520 hours at half the federal minimum wage, averaged over the income year. Apart from the minimum threshold, we do not trim earnings or use income-quality flags, and we do not require positive work weeks or hours. We construct the sample and estimate the models without weights. The threshold excludes only 0.9 percent of the SRC observations, but these observations have extreme log earnings and dominate the tails of earnings changes. 5 5 5 Without the threshold, the excess kurtosis of two-year changes in the SRC sample is 32.70 32.70 instead of 10.82 10.82 . If we also include the Census and immigrant samples, the corresponding values are 26.07 26.07 and 9.11 9.11 . Before estimating the earnings dynamics model, we remove predictable age–education–year variation from annual log earnings. Let Y i ​ t > 0 Y_{it}>0 be the selected annual labor earnings and let G i ​ t ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } G_{it}\in\{1,2,3,4\} denote completed education: less than high school, high school, some college, or BA or more. Following Karahan & Ozkan (2013c) , we use an education-specific cubic age profile and additive income-year effects. With centered and scaled age z i ​ t ≔ ( a i ​ t − 45 ) / 10 z_{it}\coloneqq(a_{it}-45)/10 , we estimate by ordinary least squares log Y i ​ t = δ t + ∑ g = 1 4 𝟏 { G i ​ t = g } ∑ p = 0 3 γ g ​ p z i ​ t p + e i ​ t , \log Y_{it}=\delta_{t}+\sum_{g=1}^{4}\mathbf{1}\{G_{it}=g\}\sum_{p=0}^{3}\gamma_{gp}z_{it}^{p}+e_{it}, (3.1) where δ t \delta_{t} is an income-year effect, which we normalize to zero in 1996. 6 6 6 We use education-specific cubics for parsimony: replacing them with separate indicators for each combination of exact age and education group increases the number of coefficients from 29 to 137, but raises the first-stage R 2 R^{2} only from 0.1890 0.1890 to 0.1917 0.1917 . We use the OLS residual u i ​ t ≔ e ^ i ​ t u_{it}\coloneqq\widehat{e}_{it} as our outcome, omitting individual fixed effects so that it retains the persistent heterogeneity modeled below. The year effects absorb common price-level changes, so deflating earnings by a year-specific price index leaves the residuals unchanged apart from numerical rounding.

sections.heading: 3.2 Gaussian benchmark
sections.text: We use a Gaussian persistent–transitory model as a natural benchmark, given its widespread use in the earnings-dynamics literature ( Abowd & Card, 1989c ; Meghir & Pistaferri, 2011c ) . We first assess how permanent heterogeneity and initial dispersion affect estimated persistence. At elapsed age t t since 30, the persistent component follows the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process d X i ( t ) = − κ X i ( t ) d t + σ d B i ( t ) , \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{i}(t)=-\kappa X_{i}(t)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}B_{i}(t), (3.2) where κ > 0 \kappa>0 controls the speed of mean reversion, σ > 0 \sigma>0 is the instantaneous volatility of persistent shocks, and B i B_{i} are independent standard Brownian motions. We assume X i ​ ( 0 ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 0 2 ) X_{i}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}) , with initial standard deviation σ 0 > 0 \sigma_{0}>0 . Persistence over an observation gap Δ > 0 \Delta>0 is e − κ ​ Δ \mathrm{e}^{-\kappa\Delta} . The stationary standard deviation is ω ≔ σ / 2 ​ κ \omega\coloneqq\sigma/\sqrt{2\kappa} ; estimating σ 0 \sigma_{0} freely allows dispersion at age 30 to differ from this long-run value. In specification (1) of Table 2 , we omit permanent effects and write u i ​ j = X i ​ ( t i ​ j ) + ϵ i ​ j , ϵ i ​ j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ϵ 2 ) . u_{ij}=X_{i}(t_{ij})+\epsilon_{ij},\qquad\epsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\epsilon}^{2}). (3.3) The transitory shocks are independent across people and dates and independent of the initial state and Brownian motions. They capture both genuine short-lived earnings changes and reporting error, which is substantial in survey earnings data ( Bound et al., 1994c ) . We apply the Kalman filter to evaluate the Gaussian levels likelihood exactly, using the actual observation gaps. We obtain κ ^ = 0.039 \widehat{\kappa}=0.039 , implying a mean-reversion half-life of about 18 years. Table 2: OU estimates under alternative permanent effects and initial conditions. sections.heading: 3.3 Earnings levels and permanent heterogeneity
sections.text: With Gaussian initial conditions and permanent heterogeneity, the OU benchmark implies a Gaussian distribution of adjusted log earnings at each fixed age. To accommodate the power-law patterns documented in the income distribution literature ( Toda, 2012c ) , we consider the normal–Laplace distribution ( Reed & Jorgensen, 2004c ) . It is the convolution of a Gaussian variable and an asymmetric Laplace variable. Exponentiating a normal–Laplace variable gives the double Pareto-lognormal distribution, whose upper and lower tails obey power laws. We fit both distributions separately within broad age groups and compare their quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plots in Figure 1 . The normal–Laplace fit improves most clearly in the lower tail and is also closer to the data between standardized log-earnings quantiles − 2 -2 and 2 2 . Discrepancies remain at the most extreme quantiles. These are descriptive marginal fits: pooling ages with different variances can produce a non-Gaussian mixture even under Gaussian OU dynamics. The plots do not by themselves establish Pareto-tail asymptotics or identify the source of non-Gaussianity. Figure 1: Standardized log-earnings quantiles by age. Note: The horizontal axis gives standard normal quantiles. Black circles show empirical quantiles and solid gray curves show quantiles of the normal–Laplace distribution that we fit by maximum likelihood within each age group. We standardize both using the empirical mean and standard deviation (with divisor n g n_{g} , the number of observations in age group g g ). The dashed gray 45-degree line gives the fitted Gaussian quantiles under the same standardization. Probabilities range from 0.0005 0.0005 to 0.9995 0.9995 ; all panels use common axis limits. We assess permanent heterogeneity as a potential source of non-Gaussian earnings levels using the panel likelihood. In specification (5) of Table 2 , we add an asymmetric Laplace component to the Gaussian intercept in (4), retaining Gaussian persistent and transitory shocks: α i ≔ G i + V a , i − V b , i − 1 / a + 1 / b , \displaystyle\alpha_{i}\coloneqq G_{i}+V_{a,i}-V_{b,i}-1/a+1/b, (3.5a) G i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ G 2 ) , V a , i ∼ Exp ⁡ ( a ) , V b , i ∼ Exp ⁡ ( b ) , \displaystyle G_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{G}^{2}),\quad V_{a,i}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(a),\quad V_{b,i}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(b), (3.5b) where G i , V a , i , V b , i G_{i},V_{a,i},V_{b,i} are mutually independent and independent of the OU process and transitory shocks. The exponential distributions use rates a , b > 0 a,b>0 , which govern the upper and lower tails, respectively. Centering ensures E ⁡ [ α i ] = 0 \E[\alpha_{i}]=0 , and Var ⁡ ( α i ) = σ G 2 + a − 2 + b − 2 \var(\alpha_{i})=\sigma_{G}^{2}+a^{-2}+b^{-2} . At each fixed age, adjusted log earnings then have a normal–Laplace distribution. This specification assigns the non-Gaussian tails to permanent heterogeneity while preserving Gaussian persistent innovations. It nests specification (4) as a , b → ∞ a,b\to\infty . In (5), we obtain a log-likelihood gain of 94.93 94.93 over (4) with two additional parameters, lowering AIC by 185.87 185.87 . 8 8 8 We evaluate the panel likelihood exactly: conditional on the asymmetric-Laplace component of α i \alpha_{i} , the model is Gaussian, and the remaining integral has a closed-form expression. See Appendix C . The Gaussian intercept component is at its zero boundary, and b ^ = 2.790 < a ^ = 3.807 \widehat{b}=2.790<\widehat{a}=3.807 implies a heavier lower tail. We also obtain faster mean reversion, κ ^ = 0.080 \widehat{\kappa}=0.080 , with a half-life of 8.7 years. Non-Gaussian permanent heterogeneity therefore improves fit and reduces the persistence attributed to the OU state. We next examine whether it also accounts for earnings dynamics.

sections.heading: 3.4 Limitations of the Gaussian OU benchmark
sections.text: We assess the joint restriction of Gaussian persistent dynamics and Gaussian transitory shocks, retaining non-Gaussian permanent heterogeneity. We examine two-year changes, conditional means and variances, and reversals after large losses and gains. We compare the data with 300 panels that we simulate from specification (5) on the observed age schedules, using its freely estimated initial dispersion. The data provide 22,619 two-year pairs and 17,586 triples with two successive two-year intervals.

sections.heading: Heavy-tailed changes
sections.text: Differencing eliminates α i \alpha_{i} regardless of its distribution, leaving the persistent and transitory components, both Gaussian under the benchmark. Let ρ ≔ e − κ \rho\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa} and η i ​ ( t ) \eta_{i}(t) denote annual persistence and Gaussian OU innovation over two years. The change satisfies d i ​ ( t ) ≔ u i ​ ( t + 2 ) − u i ​ ( t ) = ( ρ 2 − 1 ) ​ X i ​ ( t ) + η i ​ ( t ) + ϵ i ​ ( t + 2 ) − ϵ i ​ ( t ) . d_{i}(t)\coloneqq u_{i}(t+2)-u_{i}(t)=(\rho^{2}-1)X_{i}(t)+\eta_{i}(t)+\epsilon_{i}(t+2)-\epsilon_{i}(t). (3.6) At a fixed initial age, d i ​ ( t ) d_{i}(t) is therefore Gaussian. In Figure 2 , we confront this prediction with the data. Both tails of the change distribution depart sharply from the Gaussian reference. Excess kurtosis is 10.82 10.82 , compared with approximately zero in the simulated panels (Table 3 ). Pooling ages can mix Gaussian distributions with different variances, which is why the figure also shows the simulated envelope on the actual age schedules. That envelope remains close to the Gaussian reference and far from the empirical tails. The fitted benchmark therefore misses large changes despite allowing non-Gaussian permanent heterogeneity. Figure 2: Q–Q plot of two-year changes in annual log-earnings residuals. Note: We plot change quantiles against standard normal quantiles, demeaning and standardizing changes by their own standard deviation in the data and in each simulated panel. Probabilities range from 0.0005 0.0005 to 0.9995 0.9995 ; the dashed line is the Gaussian reference. For the benchmark comparisons in this section, we report medians and pointwise 95 percent ranges (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) across 300 panels that we simulate at the fitted parameters on the observed age schedules, excluding parameter uncertainty. In these simulation figures, thin black lines with circles denote the data; blue dashed lines (where shown) and bands give the simulation medians and ranges, respectively. We use specification (5) here.

sections.heading: Conditional mean and dispersion
sections.text: Figure 3 reports the mean (left) and variance (right) of earnings residuals two years later, conditional on the current residual. Within-bin linear regressions give the mean at the bin midpoint and the variance around the fitted line. The conditional mean rises with current earnings, but the fitted OU model does not reproduce its shape. The benchmark predicts too much downward adjustment at high earnings and too little recovery at very low earnings. Conditional variance is U-shaped, with dispersion rising toward both tails, especially on the lower side. The fitted benchmark gives a much flatter profile, overstating central dispersion and missing the sharp increase at low earnings. These comparisons concern the observed residual u i ​ t u_{it} , rather than the latent state X i ​ ( t ) X_{i}(t) . The OU state has a linear conditional mean and a transition variance independent of its current value. With asymmetric, non-Gaussian permanent heterogeneity, however, the composition of α i \alpha_{i} , X i ​ ( t ) X_{i}(t) , and transitory noise varies with u i ​ t u_{it} . The observed conditional mean need not be linear, nor its conditional variance flat. We simulate the fitted model with all these components to obtain the relevant comparison. Yet, its permanent heterogeneity does not account for the observed conditional profiles. Figure 3: Conditional mean and variance of annual log-earnings residuals two years later. Note: Within each bin of width 0.25, we regress the next residual on a constant and the current residual. The left panel plots the fitted mean at the bin midpoint; the right plots the residual variance, using divisor n − 2 n-2 . We only show bins with at least 100 empirical pairs. Black error bars are pointwise 95 percent percentile intervals from 500 individual-cluster bootstrap samples. We apply the same bins and estimators to panels simulated from specification (5), using the conventions of Figure 2 . The dashed line in the left panel is the 45-degree line.

sections.heading: Asymmetric reversals
sections.text: Conditional variance describes the size of future fluctuations, but not whether earnings tend to reverse direction after a large move. Gaussian mean reversion and Gaussian transitory noise can generate reversals, yet they treat positive and negative moves symmetrically: reversing both signs leaves the joint distribution of successive changes unchanged, even after pooling ages. The benchmark therefore predicts the same reversal probability after gains and losses of equal magnitude in log points. This provides a third diagnostic. To define a large move, we ask whether adjusted earnings, exp ⁡ ( u i ​ ( t ) ) \exp(u_{i}(t)) , fall to at most half their previous level or at least double. These events correspond to d i ​ ( t ) ≤ log ⁡ ( 1 / 2 ) = − log ⁡ 2 d_{i}(t)\leq\log(1/2)=-\log 2 and d i ​ ( t ) ≥ log ⁡ 2 d_{i}(t)\geq\log 2 , respectively. These thresholds have equal magnitude and opposite signs in logs. We call the next two-year change a reversal if it has the opposite sign; this does not require earnings to return fully to their previous level. Table 3 shows that the data violate the symmetry prediction. The next change reverses direction after 78.6 % 78.6\% of large losses but only 59.6 % 59.6\% of large gains, compared with simulated medians of about 74.0 % 74.0\% for both. The empirical loss–gain difference is 19.0 19.0 percentage points, with a 95 percent individual-cluster bootstrap interval of [ 14.5 , 23.7 ] [14.5,23.7] . The asymmetry also concerns the amount recovered: earnings retrace at least half of the initial log change after 53.5 % 53.5\% of large losses but only 25.1 % 25.1\% of large gains. The diagnostics leave open whether persistent dynamics, transitory shocks, or both require a richer specification. Table 3: Annual earnings dynamics: data and the Gaussian OU benchmark. sections.heading: 4 Models and estimation
sections.text: We compare four models of adjusted log earnings.

sections.heading: 4.1 Model specifications
sections.text: Throughout, t t measures years since age 30, and X i ​ t ≔ X i ​ ( t ) X_{it}\coloneqq X_{i}(t) at integer ages. We write annual persistence as ρ ≔ e − κ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \rho\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa}\in(0,1) , with κ > 0 \kappa>0 . The discrete-time models evolve annually, including years without an observed earnings measurement. All specifications use the centered asymmetric Laplace permanent effect in ( 3.5 ), imposing σ G = 0 \sigma_{G}=0 and estimating the tail rates a , b > 0 a,b>0 . We initialize X i ​ ( 0 ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 0 2 ) X_{i}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}) with a freely estimated σ 0 > 0 \sigma_{0}>0 and propagate this law to each individual’s entry age. The transition laws admit stationary distributions; the age-30 law need not be stationary. We reestimate all parameters within each specification. Our baseline observation equation is u i ​ j = α i + X i ​ ( t i ​ j ) + ϵ i ​ j . u_{ij}=\alpha_{i}+X_{i}(t_{ij})+\epsilon_{ij}. (4.1) One specification adds a shared loss component, as described below. In every model, the independent transitory shock is either ϵ i ​ j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ϵ 2 ) \epsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\epsilon}^{2}) or ϵ i ​ j ∼ ℳ ⁡ ( p ϵ , δ ϵ , σ ϵ , 1 , σ ϵ , 2 ) \epsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{M}(p_{\epsilon},\delta_{\epsilon},\sigma_{\epsilon,1},\sigma_{\epsilon,2}) , where ℳ ⁡ ( p , δ , σ 1 , σ 2 ) ≔ p ​ 𝒩 ​ ( − ( 1 − p ) ​ δ , σ 1 2 ) + ( 1 − p ) ​ 𝒩 ​ ( p ​ δ , σ 2 2 ) \mathcal{M}(p,\delta,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\coloneqq p\,\mathcal{N}(-(1-p)\delta,\sigma_{1}^{2})+(1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(p\delta,\sigma_{2}^{2}) (4.2) denotes a centered two-component Gaussian mixture, with 0 < p < 1 0<p<1 , δ ≥ 0 \delta\geq 0 , and σ 1 , σ 2 > 0 \sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}>0 . This four-parameter mixture has mean zero and ordered component means; it adds three parameters relative to Gaussian transitory noise. Individuals are independent. Within each model, permanent effects, initial states, Brownian motions, and the iid primitive shock sequences are mutually independent. We begin with the Gaussian OU process for the persistent state. GKOS, GMR, and PLV introduce non-Gaussian risk through mixture innovations, losses and scarring, and state-dependent variance, respectively.

sections.heading: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process
sections.text: The OU state follows ( 3.2 ). At annual dates, it is exactly a Gaussian AR(1) with persistence ρ \rho and innovation variance σ 2 ​ ( 1 − ρ 2 ) / ( 2 ​ κ ) \sigma^{2}(1-\rho^{2})/(2\kappa) .

sections.heading: Guvenen–Karahan–Ozkan–Song (GKOS) process
sections.text: We adapt the constant-mixture specification (Model 3) of Guvenen et al. (2021g) by introducing mean reversion. The persistent state follows X i ​ t = ρ ​ X i , t − 1 + η i ​ t , η i ​ t ∼ ℳ ⁡ ( p η , δ η , σ η , 1 , σ η , 2 ) . X_{it}=\rho X_{i,t-1}+\eta_{it},\qquad\eta_{it}\sim\mathcal{M}(p_{\eta},\delta_{\eta},\sigma_{\eta,1},\sigma_{\eta,2}). (4.3) At the boundary p η ∈ { 0 , 1 } p_{\eta}\in\{0,1\} , innovations are Gaussian; matching the component variance to the OU innovation variance recovers the exact annual OU state transition. The mixture probability p η p_{\eta} and its component distributions are constant across ages and earnings levels. Unequal component means and variances allow skewness and excess kurtosis in persistent innovations while preserving linear conditional mean reversion.

sections.heading: Guvenen–McKay–Ryan (GMR) process
sections.text: We adapt the nonemployment and scarring specification (Model 2) of Guvenen et al. (2026g) , replacing its random walk with mean reversion and adding the common independent transitory shock. Retaining their notation, let ζ i ​ t = { 0 , with probability ​ p ζ , log ⁡ ( 1 − ℓ i ​ t ) , with probability ​ 1 − p ζ , c i ​ t ≔ ζ i ​ t − E ⁡ [ ζ i ​ t ] , \zeta_{it}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{with probability }p_{\zeta},\\ \log(1-\ell_{it}),&\text{with probability }1-p_{\zeta},\end{cases}\qquad c_{it}\coloneqq\zeta_{it}-\E[\zeta_{it}], (4.4) where 0 < p ζ < 1 0<p_{\zeta}<1 and ℓ i ​ t \ell_{it} has an exponential distribution with rate λ > 0 \lambda>0 , conditional on 0 < ℓ i ​ t < 1 0<\ell_{it}<1 . Centering accommodates the zero-mean earnings residuals. sections.heading: Piecewise linear variance (PLV) process
sections.text: The heavy-tailed changes and U-shaped conditional dispersion in § 3.4 motivate a parsimonious specification with linear mean reversion and instantaneous variance that can increase with the persistent state’s distance from zero, at different rates on either side. For x ∈ ℝ x\in\mathbb{R} , let x + ≔ max ⁡ { x , 0 } x^{+}\coloneqq\max\{x,0\} and x − ≔ max ⁡ { − x , 0 } x^{-}\coloneqq\max\{-x,0\} be the positive and negative parts of x x . We define the instantaneous variance function v ⁡ ( x ) ≔ σ 2 + c + ​ x + + c − ​ x − , v(x)\coloneqq\sigma^{2}+c_{+}x^{+}+c_{-}x^{-}, (4.6) where σ > 0 \sigma>0 and c + , c − ≥ 0 c_{+},c_{-}\geq 0 . The persistent component follows the diffusion d X i ( t ) = − κ X i ( t ) d t + v ​ ( X i ​ ( t ) ) d B i ( t ) , \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{i}(t)=-\kappa X_{i}(t)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{v(X_{i}(t))}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}B_{i}(t), (4.7) where B i B_{i} is a standard Brownian motion. Setting c + = c − = 0 c_{+}=c_{-}=0 recovers the OU process. PLV belongs to the class of diffusions with linear mean reversion studied by Bibby et al. (2005c) . Its variance is affine on each half-line. When both slopes are positive, v ⁡ ( x ) v(x) is V-shaped, with its minimum at zero; c − > c + c_{-}>c_{+} makes variance rise more steeply at negative persistent states. Proposition A.1 gives exponential stationary tails on each side with a positive slope. Proposition A.2 shows that PLV preserves the conditional mean of OU, E ⁡ [ X ⁡ ( t + h ) ∣ X ⁡ ( t ) = x ] = e − κ ​ h ​ x \E[X(t+h)\mid X(t)=x]=\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa h}x , while stationary latent changes have positive limiting excess kurtosis as h ↓ 0 h\downarrow 0 whenever c + + c − > 0 c_{+}+c_{-}>0 . Proposition A.3 shows that stationary latent and observed changes remain symmetric even when the level distribution is skewed. However, it does not imply equal reversal probabilities after equally large gains and losses; unequal slopes or asymmetric transitory shocks can break the additional sign symmetry.

sections.heading: Covariance equivalence
sections.text: The four processes can share the stationary covariances targeted in earnings calibrations (e.g., Storesletten et al., 2004c ) . Proposition 4.1 (Covariance equivalence) . Consider stationary versions of the GKOS, GMR, and PLV models, with the observation equation ( 4.1 ) (including the shared loss in GMR) and any transitory-shock distribution with finite variance. For each such specification, there is a stationary OU specification with the same persistence ρ \rho and the same permanent-effect variance whose observed residuals have the same mean and the same autocovariance function at all integer lags. See the derivations following Proposition A.2 in Appendix A for the proof. The models can share stationary covariances while differing in conditional earnings risk.

sections.heading: 4.2 Likelihood estimation
sections.text: We estimate all eight specifications using the HMM likelihood in § 2 . The likelihood conditions on each individual’s observed ages and gaps, under the observation-schedule independence assumption in § 2.1 . Let θ \theta collect the parameters of the specification we estimate. We approximate the persistent state by a finite-state Markov chain while leaving earnings continuous. We use conditional moment matching ( Farmer & Toda, 2017g ) for OU, GKOS, and the Gaussian autoregressive step in GMR, and a generator approximation for PLV (Appendix D ). Conditional on the permanent effect α i = α \alpha_{i}=\alpha , OU, GKOS, and PLV have observation density f ϵ , θ ​ ( u i ​ j − α − x ) f_{\epsilon,\theta}(u_{ij}-\alpha-x) , where f ϵ , θ f_{\epsilon,\theta} is the Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture density in § 4.1 . For GMR, we use a joint transition and observation kernel that integrates its shared loss and preserves the dependence between current earnings and the persistent state. The HMM forward updates in ( 2.6 )–( 2.8 ) give the conditional whole-history likelihood L i , N ​ ( θ ∣ α ) L_{i,N}(\theta\mid\alpha) on an N N -point state grid. We integrate the whole-history likelihood over the common centered asymmetric-Laplace density f α , θ f_{\alpha,\theta} . Let K α K_{\alpha} denote the number of quadrature nodes for the permanent effect, with α i ​ k ​ ( θ ) \alpha_{ik}(\theta) the k k th node for individual i i . The exact individual likelihood and its numerical approximation are L i ​ ( θ ) \displaystyle L_{i}(\theta) = ∫ ℝ L i ​ ( θ ∣ α ) ​ f α , θ ​ ( α ) ​ ⁡ 𝑑 α , \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}L_{i}(\theta\mid\alpha)f_{\alpha,\theta}(\alpha)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\alpha, (4.8a) L i , N , K α ​ ( θ ) \displaystyle L_{i,N,K_{\alpha}}(\theta) ≔ ∑ k = 1 K α w i ​ k ​ ( θ ) ​ L i , N ​ ( θ ∣ α i ​ k ​ ( θ ) ) , \displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\alpha}}w_{ik}(\theta)L_{i,N}(\theta\mid\alpha_{ik}(\theta)), (4.8b) where each effective weight w i ​ k ​ ( θ ) w_{ik}(\theta) includes the quadrature weight and the permanent-effect density at that node. We use individual-specific nodes to resolve each history’s integrand while retaining a common prior. Appendix D.3 describes the quadrature, parameter transformations, and optimization. We jointly estimate the dynamic parameters, initial dispersion, transitory-shock distribution, and permanent-effect tail rates by maximizing the sum of individual log likelihoods, as in ( 2.9 ). For model comparison, we treat individuals as independent sampling units and the first-stage adjustment in ( 3.1 ) as fixed. Table 15 reports the available grid, range, and quadrature refinements at the empirical estimates; Appendix D.4 documents the validation and scope of these checks.

sections.heading: 4.4 Fit diagnostics
sections.text: We compare the data with 100 panels simulated from each specification at the estimates in Table 4 . The panels retain the observed ages and gaps, start from the estimated Gaussian law at age 30, and evolve annually through unobserved years. For OU, GKOS, and GMR, we simulate the exact processes at the estimated parameters. For PLV, we use 100 steps per year, each an exact Ornstein–Uhlenbeck step with the variance held at its value at the start of the step. Dynamic statistics follow § 3.4 .

sections.heading: Earnings levels
sections.text: Figure 4 shows that mixture transitory shocks improve the fit to earnings levels, although tail discrepancies remain. The central quantiles are broadly similar across models. With Gaussian transitory shocks, GKOS comes closest to the most extreme lower quantiles, while GMR and PLV produce too heavy a lower tail. Mixture shocks reduce these discrepancies, but PLV’s lower tail remains too heavy after age 40. All models understate the most extreme upper quantiles after age 40, with mixture PLV coming closest. Figure 4: Standardized log-earnings quantiles by model and age. Note: Columns are age groups; rows use Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture independent transitory shocks. Model curves are pointwise medians across 100 simulated panels. We standardize empirical and model quantiles using each age group’s empirical mean and standard deviation. Probabilities range from 0.0005 0.0005 to 0.9995 0.9995 . The dashed gray line is the Gaussian reference; all panels use common axis limits.

sections.heading: Heavy-tailed changes
sections.text: Permanent effects cancel in earnings changes, so Figure 5 isolates the persistent and transitory components. With Gaussian transitory shocks, OU and GKOS produce tails that are too thin, while GMR and PLV produce tails that are too heavy. Mixture transitory shocks generate heavy-tailed changes even under OU, but all four mixture specifications understate the most extreme standardized changes. Figure 5: Two-year log-earnings changes under the four models. Note: The left and right panels use Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture independent transitory shocks, respectively. We demean and standardize changes by their own standard deviation in the data and each simulated panel. Quantile probabilities and simulation medians follow Figure 4 . The dashed gray line is the Gaussian reference.

sections.heading: Conditional mean and dispersion
sections.text: Figure 6 shows that the conditional variance profile also depends on the transitory specification. With Gaussian transitory shocks, GMR and PLV generate a pronounced rise at low earnings. PLV overstates this rise at the lower extreme, and GMR overstates dispersion at central earnings. No Gaussian specification generates the rise at high earnings. With mixture shocks, all four models, including OU, produce a U-shaped variance profile. Thus a U-shaped profile alone does not identify state-dependent persistent volatility. Mixture PLV fits the center most closely but overstates variance at the lower extreme, and all four models understate variance at the upper end. The conditional means track the data through the central and upper bins. In the lowest bins, mixture OU predicts too much recovery and mixture PLV too little. Note: Rows use Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture independent transitory shocks; columns, bins, estimators, and empirical confidence intervals follow Figure 3 . Model curves are pointwise medians across 100 simulated panels. Dashed lines in the mean panels are 45-degree lines.

sections.heading: 5 Economic consequences of model choice
sections.text: We now ask how the choice of earnings process and the method used to discipline that process change saving and welfare. We use a deliberately simple saving problem to measure how alternative earnings inputs change economic predictions while holding preferences, prices, and mean resources fixed. We first compare the fitted processes and counterfactual processes with a common log-earnings covariance function. We then calibrate each model to moments of earnings changes and levels and compare the economic implications with those of the likelihood estimates. The main results use Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks. Allowing mixtures improves the log likelihood by more than 1,500 points in every model relative to Gaussian transitory shocks (§ 4.3 ).

sections.heading: 5.1 Saving under alternative earnings dynamics
sections.text: Households maximize E ∑ t = 0 ∞ β t u ( c t ) \E\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t}u(c_{t}) subject to a t + 1 = R ​ a t + Y t − c t ≥ 0 , c t > 0 , a_{t+1}=Ra_{t}+Y_{t}-c_{t}\geq 0,\qquad c_{t}>0, where u ⁡ ( c ) ≔ c 1 − γ / ( 1 − γ ) u(c)\coloneqq c^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma) . We set β = 0.96 \beta=0.96 , γ = 2 \gamma=2 , and R = 1.02 R=1.02 . Households observe their persistent state and current income. To isolate risk over time, we set permanent effects to zero and use stationary earnings states. We treat the transitory shock ϵ \epsilon as earnings risk in every model. 9 9 9 Part of the transitory shock in survey data is likely reporting error ( Bound et al., 1994c ) , which affects measured but not actual earnings. Treating the entire shock as earnings risk therefore overstates transitory income risk. We normalize mean raw earnings to E ⁡ y t = 1 \E y_{t}=1 and set total income to Y t = y t + b Y_{t}=y_{t}+b , with b = 0.1 b=0.1 . The transfer is thus 10 % 10\% of mean raw earnings. 10 10 10 For comparison, the 2022 federal poverty guideline for a one-person household in the contiguous states and District of Columbia was $13,590 ( U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2022c ) , about 15 % 15\% of mean annual earnings of $92,832 in our 2022 PSID sample. This common income floor also ensures finite optimal value despite the heavy lower earnings tails with PLV. We measure precautionary wealth by stationary mean assets. sections.heading: 5.2 Calibrating to moments of earnings changes and levels
sections.text: The covariance-matched results show what second moments leave undetermined. We next ask whether targeting higher moments, tail statistics, conditional moments, and moments of levels resolves these economic differences. Recent calibrations use such targets ( Guvenen et al., 2021g ; Guvenen et al., 2026g ) . We follow their designs as closely as our biennial panel allows and calibrate each model, with Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks, to 70 moments of the earnings residuals in ( 3.1 ). Table 8 groups the targets into eight sets. Sets 1–2 contain the standard deviation, skewness, and excess kurtosis of two- and six-year changes by age and recent earnings (RE), as in Guvenen et al. (2021g) . We use three age groups (30–39, 40–49, and 50–60) and measure recent earnings by the tercile of the residual within its age group. Sets 3–4 contain mean subsequent changes after extreme two-year changes, which approximate the short- and long-horizon impulse responses in Guvenen et al. (2021g) . Sets 5–6 contain the 10th and 90th percentiles and the tail probabilities of changes, as in Guvenen et al. (2026g) . Sets 7–8 contain moments of earnings levels by age: the variance and autocovariances of log earnings, which both papers target in the form of the variance over the life cycle, and the 10th and 90th percentiles. Because the targets include levels, we calibrate the initial dispersion σ 0 \sigma_{0} and the permanent-effect rates ( a , b ) (a,b) together with the dynamic and transitory parameters. We minimize a weighted sum of squared relative discrepancies, giving equal weight to each set and equal weight within sets. We fixed the targets and weights before computing any results. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Quantitative macroeconomics usually disciplines models by calibration to selected moments. Calibration is transparent, but it uses only part of the information in the data. We showed that the HMM approach makes likelihood estimation feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes with permanent heterogeneity and irregular observation dates, and that the likelihood leads to different economic answers. Our application yields three results. First, the likelihood ranks four earnings processes that can share the same covariance function: PLV and GKOS fit the data better than GMR and OU. Second, close target fit does not extend to complete earnings histories. Calibrations to 70 moments of earnings changes and levels, in the style of Guvenen et al. (2021g) ; Guvenen et al. (2026g) , fit the histories worse than every likelihood-estimated specification with mixture transitory shocks, including OU, whose persistent dynamics are Gaussian. Third, the method of choosing parameters changes the economic answer. In the same saving model, every calibration implies less wealth than the corresponding likelihood estimate, and calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of 2.5 to 3.7. Even the direction depends on the targets: when we target changes only, calibrated GKOS and GMR imply more than twice the wealth of their likelihood estimates. The likelihood is not a substitute for economic judgment. Every model we consider is misspecified, and the likelihood-preferred specifications still miss features of the data, such as the extreme kurtosis of earnings changes. However, the likelihood provides a common scale on which to compare misspecified models. We therefore recommend that quantitative studies compare candidate models by their likelihood before using them for counterfactual and policy analysis, and use targeted moments to diagnose where the selected model fails.

A regular one-dimensional diffusion on an interval is symmetric with respect to its speed measure ( Kent, 1978c , Theorem 8.1) . Under the stated recurrence and conservativeness conditions, the normalized speed measure is the invariant probability law π \pi , and the stationary process is time reversible ( Kent, 1978c , Section 9) . This proves the same conclusion for observed changes. Taking successive differences gives ( A.11 ). ∎ For PLV, Proposition A.1 verifies the conditions for stationary reversibility. With unequal slopes, Gaussian age-30 initialization can yield asymmetric finite-age changes. If c + = c − c_{+}=c_{-} , reflecting X X and B B preserves the dynamics. Time reversal exchanges both the order and signs of successive changes; it does not equate reversal probabilities after equally large initial losses and gains. Unequal slopes alone do not determine the direction or size of this gap. There is a further identification restriction. Let X ~ \widetilde{X} have the slopes ( c − , c + ) (c_{-},c_{+}) in place of ( c + , c − ) (c_{+},c_{-}) and the reflected initial law. Its variance function is v ~ ​ ( x ) = v ​ ( − x ) \widetilde{v}(x)=v(-x) ; reflecting X X and B B in ( 4.7 ) and using uniqueness gives ( X ~ ​ ( t ) ) t ≥ 0 ​ = 𝑑 ​ ( − X ⁡ ( t ) ) t ≥ 0 . (\widetilde{X}(t))_{t\geq 0}\overset{d}{=}(-X(t))_{t\geq 0}. Consequently, swapping slopes preserves every latent covariance and, with the same independent permanent and transitory components, every observed covariance. This holds under the common Gaussian age-30 initialization, whose law is symmetric, as well as under the respective invariant laws. Under those invariant laws, Proposition A.3 also implies that X ~ ​ ( t + h ) − X ~ ​ ( t ) \widetilde{X}(t+h)-\widetilde{X}(t) and X ⁡ ( t + h ) − X ⁡ ( t ) X(t+h)-X(t) have the same distribution for every h > 0 h>0 . The permanent effect cancels from earnings changes, and the independent transitory difference is symmetric for any iid transitory law, including an asymmetric Gaussian mixture. Thus stationary marginal earnings-change distributions cannot distinguish the two slope orientations, even if we observe the entire distribution. Information about this orientation must come from other features, such as earnings levels, conditional profiles, or joint histories of changes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Asymptotic theory of HMM estimation
sections.text: This appendix develops the asymptotic theory that underlies the inference procedure in § 2.4 . We maintain the setting and notation of § 2 . The number of individuals I I grows, while each history remains bounded. We first fix the grid and then let it refine with I I .

sections.heading: B.1 Fixed-grid inference
sections.text: We first fix the grid 𝒳 N \mathcal{X}_{N} and let I → ∞ I\to\infty . Recall the discretized population objective 𝒬 N \mathcal{Q}_{N} , its maximizer θ N \theta_{N} , and the individual score s i , N s_{i,N} and Hessian H i , N H_{i,N} in ( 2.10 ) from § 2.4 . At fixed N N , the discretized quasi-maximum likelihood estimator is an M M -estimator. We impose standard regularity conditions. Assumption 1 (Fixed-grid regularity) . Consider the following conditions: (i) (Identification) The function 𝒬 N \mathcal{Q}_{N} is finite and continuous on the compact parameter space Θ \Theta , and its unique maximizer is θ N \theta_{N} . (ii) (Uniform convergence of criterion) The sample criterion satisfies the uniform law of large numbers plim I → ∞ sup θ ∈ Θ | 1 I ∑ i = 1 I ℓ i , N ( θ ) − 𝒬 N ( θ ) | = 0 . \plim_{I\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\lvert\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\ell_{i,N}(\theta)-\mathcal{Q}_{N}(\theta)\right\rvert=0. (iii) (Interior and smoothness) The parameter θ N \theta_{N} belongs to the interior of Θ \Theta . On an open neighborhood U ⊂ int ⁡ Θ U\subset\interior\Theta of θ N \theta_{N} , ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) \ell_{i,N}(\theta) is twice continuously differentiable in θ \theta almost surely. (iv) (Score regularity) Differentiation under the expectation is valid at θ N \theta_{N} , and E 0 ⁡ ∥ s i , N ​ ( θ N ) ∥ 2 < ∞ \E_{0}\lVert s_{i,N}(\theta_{N})\rVert^{2}<\infty . (v) (Uniform convergence of Hessian) The expected Hessian E 0 ⁡ [ H i , N ​ ( θ ) ] \E_{0}[H_{i,N}(\theta)] is continuous at θ N \theta_{N} , and the sample Hessian satisfies the uniform law of large numbers plim I → ∞ sup θ ∈ U ‖ 1 I ∑ i = 1 I H i , N ( θ ) − E 0 [ H i , N ( θ ) ] ‖ = 0 . \plim_{I\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in U}\left\lVert\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}H_{i,N}(\theta)-\E_{0}[H_{i,N}(\theta)]\right\rVert=0. (vi) (Nonsingularity) The matrix A N ≔ − E 0 ⁡ [ H i , N ​ ( θ N ) ] A_{N}\coloneqq-\E_{0}[H_{i,N}(\theta_{N})] is nonsingular. These conditions yield the standard consistency and asymptotic normality results for the discretized M M -estimator at a fixed grid. Assumption 1 is deliberately high-level but standard for smooth finite-dimensional M M -estimation. Conditions (i) – (ii) deliver consistency, while the remaining conditions permit a quadratic expansion and a central limit theorem. At a fixed grid, they typically follow from smooth transition probabilities and observation densities, suitable integrable envelopes, and local identification. In the earnings model below, we use a Gaussian observation density and integrate over permanent heterogeneity before forming the individual log likelihood. Proposition B.1 (Fixed-grid consistency) . Under Assumption 1 (i) – (ii) , we have plim I → ∞ θ ^ I , N = θ N \plim_{I\to\infty}\widehat{\theta}_{I,N}=\theta_{N} . Proof. This is an application of the argmax consistency theorem ( Vaart, 1998c , Theorem 5.7) . ∎ Proposition B.2 (Fixed-grid asymptotic normality) . Under Assumption 1 (i) – (vi) , letting B N ≔ E 0 ⁡ [ s i , N ​ ( θ N ) ​ s i , N ​ ( θ N ) ⊤ ] B_{N}\coloneqq\E_{0}[s_{i,N}(\theta_{N})s_{i,N}(\theta_{N})^{\top}] , as I → ∞ I\to\infty we have I ​ ( θ ^ I , N − θ N ) → d 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , A N − 1 ​ B N ​ A N − 1 ) . \sqrt{I}(\widehat{\theta}_{I,N}-\theta_{N})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,A_{N}^{-1}B_{N}A_{N}^{-1}). (B.1) Proof. This follows from the standard argument for smooth M M -estimators, analogous to Vaart (1998c, Theorem 5.23) . ∎ Even when the continuous-state model is correct, its finite-grid likelihood is generally misspecified. The sandwich covariance in ( B.1 ) therefore does not ordinarily reduce to A N − 1 A_{N}^{-1} .

sections.heading: B.2 Continuous-state inference
sections.text: We now allow the grid size N N to increase with the cross-sectional sample size I I . Let N = N I → ∞ N=N_{I}\to\infty as I → ∞ I\to\infty . Consistency requires a qualitative approximation of the continuous-state likelihood, whereas inference centered at the continuous-state parameter requires a quantitative bound on the discretization error. Assumption 2 (Refining-grid regularity) . Consider the following conditions: (i) (Identification) The function 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} is finite and continuous on the compact parameter space Θ \Theta , and its unique maximizer is θ 0 \theta_{0} . (ii) (Positivity) For every θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta and sufficiently large N N , we have L i ​ ( θ ) > 0 L_{i}(\theta)>0 and L i , N ​ ( θ ) > 0 L_{i,N}(\theta)>0 almost surely. (iii) (Integrable envelope) For some integrable M i ≥ 0 M_{i}\geq 0 , | ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) | ≤ M i \lvert\ell_{i,N}(\theta)\rvert\leq M_{i} for every sufficiently large N N and θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta . (iv) (Uniform Lipschitz continuity) There is a nonnegative random variable C i C_{i} with E 0 ⁡ C i < ∞ \E_{0}C_{i}<\infty such that, for every sufficiently large N N and θ , θ ′ ∈ Θ \theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta , | ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) − ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ′ ) | ≤ C i ​ ∥ θ − θ ′ ∥ . \lvert\ell_{i,N}(\theta)-\ell_{i,N}(\theta^{\prime})\rvert\leq C_{i}\lVert\theta-\theta^{\prime}\rVert. (v) (Likelihood approximation) As N → ∞ N\to\infty , we have E 0 ⁡ [ sup θ ∈ Θ | ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) − ℓ i ​ ( θ ) | ] → 0 . \E_{0}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lvert\ell_{i,N}(\theta)-\ell_{i}(\theta)\rvert\right]\to 0. (B.2) These conditions make the discretized sample criterion converge uniformly to the continuous-state population objective as both I I and N N increase. Proposition B.3 (Continuous-state consistency) . Under Assumption 2 , for every deterministic sequence N I → ∞ N_{I}\to\infty , we have plim I → ∞ θ ^ I , N I = θ 0 \plim_{I\to\infty}\widehat{\theta}_{I,N_{I}}=\theta_{0} . Proof. Recall the sample objective 𝒬 ^ I , N \widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N} in ( 2.9 ). We first establish the triangular-array uniform law sup θ ∈ Θ | 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ ) − 𝒬 N I ​ ( θ ) | = o p ​ ( 1 ) . \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta)-\mathcal{Q}_{N_{I}}(\theta)\right\rvert=o_{\mathrm{p}}(1). Fix δ > 0 \delta>0 . Compactness of Θ \Theta gives a finite δ \delta -net { θ 1 , … , θ K } \{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{K}\} . For each θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta , choose k ⁡ ( θ ) k(\theta) such that ∥ θ − θ k ⁡ ( θ ) ∥ ≤ δ \lVert\theta-\theta_{k(\theta)}\rVert\leq\delta . Assumption 2 (iv) implies sup θ ∈ Θ | 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ ) − 𝒬 N I ​ ( θ ) | ≤ max 1 ≤ k ≤ K ⁡ | 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ k ) − 𝒬 N I ​ ( θ k ) | + δ ⁡ ( 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I C i + E 0 ⁡ C i ) . \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta)-\mathcal{Q}_{N_{I}}(\theta)\right\rvert\\ \leq\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta_{k})-\mathcal{Q}_{N_{I}}(\theta_{k})\right\rvert+\delta\left(\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}C_{i}+\E_{0}C_{i}\right). (B.3) We next show that every term in the finite maximum converges to zero in probability. Fix k k and write Z i , I ≔ ℓ i , N I ​ ( θ k ) Z_{i,I}\coloneqq\ell_{i,N_{I}}(\theta_{k}) . By Assumption 2 (iii) , | Z i , I | ≤ M i \lvert Z_{i,I}\rvert\leq M_{i} with E 0 ⁡ M i < ∞ \E_{0}M_{i}<\infty . For b > 0 b>0 , define Z i , I ( b ) ≔ Z i , I 𝟏 { M i ≤ b } Z_{i,I}^{(b)}\coloneqq Z_{i,I}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{M_{i}\leq b\right\}} . Independence across individuals and Chebyshev’s inequality give E 0 ⁡ | 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I ( Z i , I ( b ) − E 0 ⁡ Z i , I ( b ) ) | 2 ≤ b 2 I . \E_{0}\left\lvert\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(Z_{i,I}^{(b)}-\E_{0}Z_{i,I}^{(b)}\right)\right\rvert^{2}\leq\frac{b^{2}}{I}. For the discarded part, the triangle inequality yields E 0 | 1 I ∑ i = 1 I [ Z i , I − Z i , I ( b ) − E 0 ( Z i , I − Z i , I ( b ) ) ] | ≤ 2 E 0 [ M i 𝟏 { M i > b } ] . \E_{0}\left\lvert\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left[Z_{i,I}-Z_{i,I}^{(b)}-\E_{0}\left(Z_{i,I}-Z_{i,I}^{(b)}\right)\right]\right\rvert\leq 2\E_{0}[M_{i}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{M_{i}>b\right\}}]. The right-hand side tends to zero as b → ∞ b\to\infty . Taking I → ∞ I\to\infty for fixed b b and then b → ∞ b\to\infty proves 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ k ) − 𝒬 N I ​ ( θ k ) = o p ​ ( 1 ) \widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta_{k})-\mathcal{Q}_{N_{I}}(\theta_{k})=o_{\mathrm{p}}(1) . Because the net is finite, the maximum in ( B.3 ) is also o p ​ ( 1 ) o_{\mathrm{p}}(1) . The weak law also gives I − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 I C i → p E 0 ⁡ C i I^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{I}C_{i}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}\E_{0}C_{i} . We can first choose δ \delta arbitrarily small and then let I → ∞ I\to\infty in ( B.3 ), which proves the claimed uniform law. Assumption 2 (v) also implies sup θ ∈ Θ | 𝒬 N ​ ( θ ) − 𝒬 ⁡ ( θ ) | \displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lvert\mathcal{Q}_{N}(\theta)-\mathcal{Q}(\theta)\rvert ≤ E 0 ⁡ [ sup θ ∈ Θ | ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) − ℓ i ​ ( θ ) | ] → 0 . \displaystyle\leq\E_{0}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lvert\ell_{i,N}(\theta)-\ell_{i}(\theta)\rvert\right]\to 0. Consequently, sup θ ∈ Θ | 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ ) − 𝒬 ⁡ ( θ ) | = o p ​ ( 1 ) . \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta)-\mathcal{Q}(\theta)\right\rvert=o_{\mathrm{p}}(1). (B.4) It remains to apply identification. For any ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , define Θ ϵ ≔ { θ ∈ Θ : ∥ θ − θ 0 ∥ ≥ ϵ } . \Theta_{\epsilon}\coloneqq\left\{\theta\in\Theta:\lVert\theta-\theta_{0}\rVert\geq\epsilon\right\}. If Θ ϵ \Theta_{\epsilon} is nonempty, continuity of 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} , compactness of Θ ϵ \Theta_{\epsilon} , and uniqueness of its maximizer imply η ϵ ≔ 𝒬 ⁡ ( θ 0 ) − sup θ ∈ Θ ϵ 𝒬 ⁡ ( θ ) > 0 . \eta_{\epsilon}\coloneqq\mathcal{Q}(\theta_{0})-\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{\epsilon}}\mathcal{Q}(\theta)>0. On the event that the supremum in ( B.4 ) is smaller than η ϵ / 3 \eta_{\epsilon}/3 , 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ 0 ) > sup θ ∈ Θ ϵ 𝒬 ^ I , N I ​ ( θ ) . \widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta_{0})>\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{\epsilon}}\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{I,N_{I}}(\theta). Hence no maximizer of the sample objective belongs to Θ ϵ \Theta_{\epsilon} . The probability of this event tends to one by ( B.4 ), so Pr ⁡ ( ∥ θ ^ I , N I − θ 0 ∥ ≥ ϵ ) → 0 \Pr(\lVert\widehat{\theta}_{I,N_{I}}-\theta_{0}\rVert\geq\epsilon)\to 0 for every ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 . ∎ Consistency imposes no relative rate between I I and N I N_{I} . Suppose the grid becomes fine on every compact subset of the state space and its endpoints approach the boundaries. On an evenly spaced grid, standard quadrature formulas such as the composite trapezoidal and Simpson rules approximate transition integrals under familiar smoothness and tail conditions ( Davis & Rabinowitz, 1984c ) . If the resulting discrete initial distributions and transition kernels converge weakly, uniformly in θ \theta , then bounded path length, continuity, uniform integrability, and suitable control of likelihoods near zero allow the convergence to pass through the successive transition integrations and the logarithm. Obtaining ( B.2 ) requires these additional uniformity conditions because weak convergence alone does not control logarithms or parameter variation. This rate-free conclusion parallels Farmer (2021g, Theorem 5.1) . Consistency alone does not make the grid error negligible relative to the sampling error. To address this issue, define the individual score and Hessian of the exact continuous-state log likelihood by s i ​ ( θ ) ≔ ∇ ℓ i ​ ( θ ) , H i ​ ( θ ) ≔ ∇ 2 ℓ i ​ ( θ ) . s_{i}(\theta)\coloneqq\nabla\ell_{i}(\theta),\qquad H_{i}(\theta)\coloneqq\nabla^{2}\ell_{i}(\theta). In Equation ( 2.10 ), we define the corresponding discretized derivatives s i , N s_{i,N} and H i , N H_{i,N} . Assumption 3 (Continuous-state normality) . Consider the following conditions: (i) (Interior and smoothness) The parameter θ 0 \theta_{0} belongs to the interior of Θ \Theta . On an open neighborhood U ⊂ int ⁡ Θ U\subset\interior\Theta of θ 0 \theta_{0} , ℓ i ​ ( θ ) \ell_{i}(\theta) and ℓ i , N ​ ( θ ) \ell_{i,N}(\theta) are twice continuously differentiable in θ \theta almost surely for every sufficiently large N N . (ii) (Score regularity) We have E 0 ⁡ s i ​ ( θ 0 ) = 0 \E_{0}s_{i}(\theta_{0})=0 and E 0 ⁡ ∥ s i ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ 2 < ∞ \E_{0}\lVert s_{i}(\theta_{0})\rVert^{2}<\infty . (iii) (Hessian regularity) We have E ⁡ sup θ ∈ U 0 ⁡ ∥ H i ​ ( θ ) ∥ < ∞ \E_{0}\sup_{\theta\in U}\lVert H_{i}(\theta)\rVert<\infty , and plim I → ∞ sup θ ∈ U ‖ 1 I ∑ i = 1 I H i ( θ ) − E 0 H i ( θ ) ‖ = 0 . \plim_{I\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in U}\left\lVert\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}H_{i}(\theta)-\E_{0}H_{i}(\theta)\right\rVert=0. (iv) (Nonsingularity) The matrix A ≔ − E 0 ⁡ H i ​ ( θ 0 ) A\coloneqq-\E_{0}H_{i}(\theta_{0}) is nonsingular. (v) (Score approximation) As N → ∞ N\to\infty , E 0 ⁡ ∥ s i , N ​ ( θ 0 ) − s i ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ 2 → 0 . \E_{0}\lVert s_{i,N}(\theta_{0})-s_{i}(\theta_{0})\rVert^{2}\to 0. (B.5) (vi) (Hessian approximation) As N → ∞ N\to\infty , E 0 ⁡ [ sup θ ∈ U ∥ H i , N ​ ( θ ) − H i ​ ( θ ) ∥ ] → 0 . \E_{0}\left[\sup_{\theta\in U}\lVert H_{i,N}(\theta)-H_{i}(\theta)\rVert\right]\to 0. (B.6) (vii) (Score-bias rate) Along the sequence N I N_{I} , I ​ ∥ E 0 ⁡ s i , N I ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ → 0 . \sqrt{I}\lVert\E_{0}s_{i,N_{I}}(\theta_{0})\rVert\to 0. (B.7) These additional conditions make the discretization error negligible at the I \sqrt{I} scale and permit inference for the continuous-state target. Proposition B.4 (Continuous-state asymptotic normality) . Under Assumptions 2 and 3 , letting B ≔ E 0 ⁡ [ s i ​ ( θ 0 ) ​ s i ​ ( θ 0 ) ⊤ ] B\coloneqq\E_{0}[s_{i}(\theta_{0})s_{i}(\theta_{0})^{\top}] , as I → ∞ I\to\infty we have I ​ ( θ ^ I , N I − θ 0 ) → d 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , A − 1 ​ B ​ A − 1 ) . \sqrt{I}(\widehat{\theta}_{I,N_{I}}-\theta_{0})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,A^{-1}BA^{-1}). (B.8) Proof. For brevity, write θ ^ I ≔ θ ^ I , N I \widehat{\theta}_{I}\coloneqq\widehat{\theta}_{I,N_{I}} and define the approximate sample score and Hessian by S ^ I ​ ( θ ) ≔ 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I s i , N I ​ ( θ ) , H ^ I ​ ( θ ) ≔ 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I H i , N I ​ ( θ ) . \widehat{S}_{I}(\theta)\coloneqq\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}s_{i,N_{I}}(\theta),\qquad\widehat{H}_{I}(\theta)\coloneqq\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}H_{i,N_{I}}(\theta). We first derive the limiting distribution of the score at θ 0 \theta_{0} . Let d i , I ≔ s i , N I ​ ( θ 0 ) − s i ​ ( θ 0 ) d_{i,I}\coloneqq s_{i,N_{I}}(\theta_{0})-s_{i}(\theta_{0}) . Since E 0 ⁡ s i ​ ( θ 0 ) = 0 \E_{0}s_{i}(\theta_{0})=0 , we may write I ​ S ^ I ​ ( θ 0 ) = 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I s i ​ ( θ 0 ) + 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I ( d i , I − E 0 ⁡ d i , I ) + I ​ E 0 ​ s i , N I ​ ( θ 0 ) . \sqrt{I}\widehat{S}_{I}(\theta_{0})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{I}}\sum_{i=1}^{I}s_{i}(\theta_{0})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{I}}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(d_{i,I}-\E_{0}d_{i,I}\right)+\sqrt{I}\E_{0}s_{i,N_{I}}(\theta_{0}). (B.9) The first term converges in distribution to 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , B ) \mathcal{N}(0,B) by the multivariate central limit theorem. Independence across individuals and Assumption 3 (v) imply E 0 ⁡ ‖ 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I ( d i , I − E 0 ⁡ d i , I ) ‖ 2 = tr ⁡ Var 0 ⁡ ( d i , I ) ≤ E 0 ⁡ ∥ d i , I ∥ 2 → 0 . \E_{0}\left\lVert\frac{1}{\sqrt{I}}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(d_{i,I}-\E_{0}d_{i,I}\right)\right\rVert^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\var_{0}(d_{i,I})\leq\E_{0}\lVert d_{i,I}\rVert^{2}\to 0. The second term in ( B.9 ) is therefore o p ​ ( 1 ) o_{\mathrm{p}}(1) , while its third term is o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) by Assumption 3 (vii) . It follows that I ​ S ^ I ​ ( θ 0 ) → d 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , B ) . \sqrt{I}\widehat{S}_{I}(\theta_{0})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,B). (B.10) We next establish convergence of the approximate sample Hessian. Let Z i , N ≔ sup θ ∈ U ∥ H i , N ​ ( θ ) − H i ​ ( θ ) ∥ . Z_{i,N}\coloneqq\sup_{\theta\in U}\lVert H_{i,N}(\theta)-H_{i}(\theta)\rVert. By Assumption 3 (vi) and Markov’s inequality, for every ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , Pr ⁡ ( 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I Z i , N I > ϵ ) ≤ E 0 ⁡ Z i , N I ϵ → 0 . \Pr\left(\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}Z_{i,N_{I}}>\epsilon\right)\leq\frac{\E_{0}Z_{i,N_{I}}}{\epsilon}\to 0. Therefore, sup θ ∈ U ‖ H ^ I ​ ( θ ) − 1 I ​ ∑ i = 1 I H i ​ ( θ ) ‖ = o p ​ ( 1 ) . \sup_{\theta\in U}\left\lVert\widehat{H}_{I}(\theta)-\frac{1}{I}\sum_{i=1}^{I}H_{i}(\theta)\right\rVert=o_{\mathrm{p}}(1). Combining this result with Assumption 3 (iii) gives sup θ ∈ U ∥ H ^ I ​ ( θ ) − E 0 ⁡ H i ​ ( θ ) ∥ = o p ​ ( 1 ) . \sup_{\theta\in U}\lVert\widehat{H}_{I}(\theta)-\E_{0}H_{i}(\theta)\rVert=o_{\mathrm{p}}(1). (B.11) The map θ ↦ E 0 ⁡ H i ​ ( θ ) \theta\mapsto\E_{0}H_{i}(\theta) is continuous at θ 0 \theta_{0} : the Hessian is continuous almost surely by Assumption 3 (i) , and the integrable bound in Assumption 3 (iii) permits dominated convergence. By Proposition B.3 , θ ^ I \widehat{\theta}_{I} converges in probability to θ 0 \theta_{0} . Choose r > 0 r>0 so that U U contains the closed ball of radius r r centered at θ 0 \theta_{0} . With probability approaching one, θ ^ I \widehat{\theta}_{I} belongs to this ball. The interior of Θ \Theta contains the convex ball, so the estimator is interior and the line segment joining θ 0 \theta_{0} to θ ^ I \widehat{\theta}_{I} lies in U U . On this event, the first-order condition and the fundamental theorem of calculus give 0 = S ^ I ​ ( θ ^ I ) = S ^ I ​ ( θ 0 ) + H ¯ I ​ ( θ ^ I − θ 0 ) , 0=\widehat{S}_{I}(\widehat{\theta}_{I})=\widehat{S}_{I}(\theta_{0})+\bar{H}_{I}(\widehat{\theta}_{I}-\theta_{0}), (B.12) where H ¯ I ≔ ∫ 0 1 H ^ I ​ ( θ 0 + u ⁡ ( θ ^ I − θ 0 ) ) ​ ⁡ 𝑑 u . \bar{H}_{I}\coloneqq\int_{0}^{1}\widehat{H}_{I}\left(\theta_{0}+u(\widehat{\theta}_{I}-\theta_{0})\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u. Uniform convergence in ( B.11 ), continuity of E 0 ⁡ H i ​ ( θ ) \E_{0}H_{i}(\theta) at θ 0 \theta_{0} , and consistency of θ ^ I \widehat{\theta}_{I} imply H ¯ I = − A + o p ​ ( 1 ) . \bar{H}_{I}=-A+o_{\mathrm{p}}(1). (B.13) Since A A is nonsingular, H ¯ I \bar{H}_{I} is nonsingular with probability approaching one, and − H ¯ I − 1 = A − 1 + o p ​ ( 1 ) -\bar{H}_{I}^{-1}=A^{-1}+o_{\mathrm{p}}(1) . Multiplying ( B.12 ) by I \sqrt{I} and using ( B.10 ) and ( B.13 ) yields I ​ ( θ ^ I , N I − θ 0 ) = − H ¯ I − 1 ​ I ​ S ^ I ​ ( θ 0 ) → d 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , A − 1 ​ B ​ A − 1 ) . ∎ \sqrt{I}(\widehat{\theta}_{I,N_{I}}-\theta_{0})=-\bar{H}_{I}^{-1}\sqrt{I}\widehat{S}_{I}(\theta_{0})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,A^{-1}BA^{-1}).\qed When the continuous-state model is correct and the information identity holds, B = A B=A . The estimator then has asymptotic variance A − 1 A^{-1} and attains the parametric information bound for θ 0 \theta_{0} in the continuous-state model. Under misspecification, the sandwich form in ( B.8 ) applies instead. A sufficient quantitative condition for ( B.7 ) is a bound ∥ E 0 ⁡ s i , N ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ ≤ a N \lVert\E_{0}s_{i,N}(\theta_{0})\rVert\leq a_{N} with I ​ a N I → 0 \sqrt{I}a_{N_{I}}\to 0 . Under the same local curvature conditions, this score bias also bounds ∥ θ N − θ 0 ∥ \lVert\theta_{N}-\theta_{0}\rVert to first order. With bounded histories, independence lets the centered score approximation errors average out under ( B.5 ), while their mean must be o ( I − 1 / 2 ) o(I^{-1/2}) . This gives the short-panel counterpart to Farmer (2021g, Theorems 5.1 and 5.3) , whose analysis controls approximation errors along a growing time series. Additional smoothness relates the required rate to the grid. The fixed parameter dimension d θ d_{\theta} determines the dimensions of the score and Hessian but does not enter the rate condition. The state dimension d x d_{x} does enter because it determines how the mesh width varies with the total number of grid points. Consider a rectangular tensor-product grid whose coordinate ranges and resolutions are comparable. Let R N R_{N} denote the common order of its side lengths, let h N h_{N} be the largest mesh width, and let τ N \tau_{N} bound the error from truncating the state space. Since N N is the total number of grid points, a balanced grid satisfies h N ≍ R N N − 1 / d x h_{N}\asymp R_{N}N^{-1/d_{x}} . Suppose, uniformly on a neighborhood of θ 0 \theta_{0} , that for some constant C < ∞ C<\infty , we have ∥ E 0 ⁡ s i , N ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ + ( E 0 ⁡ ∥ s i , N ​ ( θ 0 ) − s i ​ ( θ 0 ) ∥ 2 ) 1 / 2 + E 0 ⁡ [ sup θ ∈ U ∥ H i , N ​ ( θ ) − H i ​ ( θ ) ∥ ] ≤ C ⁡ ( R N d x ​ h N r + τ N ) . \lVert\E_{0}s_{i,N}(\theta_{0})\rVert+\left(\E_{0}\lVert s_{i,N}(\theta_{0})-s_{i}(\theta_{0})\rVert^{2}\right)^{1/2}+\E_{0}\left[\sup_{\theta\in U}\lVert H_{i,N}(\theta)-H_{i}(\theta)\rVert\right]\\ \leq C(R_{N}^{d_{x}}h_{N}^{r}+\tau_{N}). The tensor-product composite trapezoidal rule has r = 2 r=2 when the relevant integrands have bounded second derivatives, whereas the tensor-product composite Simpson rule has r = 4 r=4 when they have bounded fourth derivatives and each coordinate has an even number of subintervals ( Davis & Rabinowitz, 1984c ) . It is therefore sufficient for centered normal inference that I ​ ( R N I d x ​ h N I r + τ N I ) → 0 . \sqrt{I}\bigl(R_{N_{I}}^{d_{x}}h_{N_{I}}^{r}+\tau_{N_{I}}\bigr)\to 0. (B.14) For a balanced grid on a compact state space, R N = O ⁡ ( 1 ) R_{N}=O(1) and τ N = 0 \tau_{N}=0 , while h N = O ( N − 1 / d x ) h_{N}=O(N^{-1/d_{x}}) . Condition ( B.14 ) then reduces to I N I − r / d x → 0 \sqrt{I}N_{I}^{-r/d_{x}}\to 0 , or equivalently N I I − d x / ( 2 r ) → ∞ N_{I}I^{-d_{x}/(2r)}\to\infty . Thus it is sufficient that N I / I d x / 4 → ∞ N_{I}/I^{d_{x}/4}\to\infty for the trapezoidal rule or N I / I d x / 8 → ∞ N_{I}/I^{d_{x}/8}\to\infty for Simpson’s rule. These are illustrative sufficient rates: to apply them to a particular HMM approximation, we must verify the stated uniform bound for its likelihood derivatives across all transition and integration approximations. Simpson’s quadrature order alone does not determine the filter’s overall accuracy. On an expanding grid, both the volume bound R N d x R_{N}^{d_{x}} and the tail error τ N \tau_{N} enter ( B.14 ). These rates describe a balanced full tensor grid, whose node count grows exponentially in d x d_{x} at a fixed resolution per coordinate. When this curse of dimensionality is consequential, sparse-grid or dimension-adaptive quadrature can reduce the number of nodes under suitable mixed-smoothness conditions ( Gerstner & Griebel, 1998c ) . The consistency and normality propositions remain applicable. To apply either proposition with such a rule, we would replace the tensor-grid bound in ( B.14 ) with the error bound for the chosen grid and quadrature rule. In the earnings application, N N discretizes the scalar persistent state and K α K_{\alpha} nodes integrate the permanent effect; approximation requirements apply jointly to both.

sections.heading: Appendix D Numerical implementation and validation
sections.text: We construct the likelihoods used in § 4.2 from known transition densities for OU, GKOS, and the Gaussian step of GMR (Appendix D.1 ). For PLV, whose transition density has no closed form, we approximate the diffusion generator (Appendix D.2 ). We also apply the generator construction to OU, whose exact likelihood provides a benchmark for numerical accuracy. Let N N denote the number of filtering nodes and K α K_{\alpha} the number of permanent-effect quadrature nodes. We therefore use the same AR(1) construction for OU and GKOS, with Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture innovations, respectively. For each starting node x n x_{n} , we set q n ​ k ∝ f η , θ ​ ( x k − ρ ​ x n ) q_{nk}\propto f_{\eta,\theta}(x_{k}-\rho x_{n}) and normalize across k k , where f η , θ f_{\eta,\theta} is the persistent innovation density. sections.text: On a uniform filtering grid with odd N N and spacing Δ ​ x \Delta x , composite Simpson weights are ( q 1 , … , q N ) \displaystyle(q_{1},\dots,q_{N}) = Δ ​ x 3 ​ ( 1 , 4 , 2 , 4 , … , 2 , 4 , 1 ) . \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta x}{3}(1,4,2,4,\dots,2,4,1). sections.heading: Initialization
sections.text: We first integrate the Gaussian initial law over the fine-grid cells C j C_{j} and normalize on the truncated interval, obtaining the row vector p θ , M , 0 p_{\theta,M,0} .
