At t i ​ 0 = 0 t_{i0}=0 , we use the Gaussian density directly on the filtering grid, with probabilities proportional to q n ​ φ ​ ( x n / σ 0 ) / σ 0 q_{n}\varphi(x_{n}/\sigma_{0})/\sigma_{0} . This initialization retains the freely estimated Gaussian initial law rather than replacing it with stationary probabilities.

sections.heading: Generator grid choices
sections.text: For PLV, we use N = 641 N=641 evenly spaced filtering nodes on [ − 8 , 8 ] [-8,8] to accommodate the greater dispersion at negative states. For the PLV generator, we use M = r ⁡ ( N − 1 ) + 1 M=r(N-1)+1 with r = 4 r=4 , so M = 2,561 M=2{,}561 and the generator spacing is 1 / 160 1/160 . The cost of the matrix exponential grows like M 3 M^{3} , so we do not refine further during estimation. Instead, we recompute the likelihood with r = 8 r=8 at the reported estimates (Table 15 ).

sections.heading: D.3 Common numerical settings and optimization
sections.text: We feed both transition constructions into the HMM likelihood. We integrate over permanent heterogeneity and optimize the resulting criterion in the same way across models. During estimation, we hold the filtering grids fixed. For OU, GKOS, and GMR, we use N = 321 N=321 evenly spaced nodes on [ − 4 , 4 ] [-4,4] , so the spacing is 1 / 40 1/40 , the same as for PLV (Appendix D.2 ). We bound each standard deviation of a transitory shock or of a GKOS innovation component below by the filtering spacing of 1 / 40 = 0.025 1/40=0.025 , because the filter must resolve the transitory density (Appendix D.4 ). At the reported estimates, we recompute the likelihood on a grid twice as fine and on a range twice as wide (Table 15 ). We use individual-specific quadrature to cover a broad range of permanent effects while resolving the region that contributes most to each integral. We obtain reference quantities from specification (5) of Table 2 at its maximum likelihood estimate θ ^ ( 5 ) \widehat{\theta}^{(5)} . This specification has a closed-form likelihood and posterior (Appendix C ). For the window, let α ^ i GLS \widehat{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{GLS}} be the generalized least squares estimate under the specification-(5) covariance and let τ i \tau_{i} be its standard error under that reference covariance. We use this reference scale to set the integration window: A i − \displaystyle A_{i}^{-} = 1.5 ​ min ⁡ { α ^ i GLS − 8 ​ τ i , − 4.5 } , \displaystyle=1.5\min\{\widehat{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{GLS}}-8\tau_{i},-4.5\}, A i + \displaystyle A_{i}^{+} = 1.5 ​ max ⁡ { α ^ i GLS + 8 ​ τ i , 4.5 } . \displaystyle=1.5\max\{\widehat{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{GLS}}+8\tau_{i},4.5\}. Separately, we compute the reference posterior moments μ i = E θ ^ ( 5 ) ⁡ [ α i ∣ 𝐮 i ] , s i 2 = Var θ ^ ( 5 ) ⁡ ( α i ∣ 𝐮 i ) . \mu_{i}=\E_{\widehat{\theta}^{(5)}}[\alpha_{i}\mid\mathbf{u}_{i}],\qquad s_{i}^{2}=\var_{\widehat{\theta}^{(5)}}(\alpha_{i}\mid\mathbf{u}_{i}). We use these moments to place nodes near the reference posterior’s mass and split at the current permanent-effect density’s mode, where its slope changes. The three interior cutpoints are μ i − 2 ​ max ​ { s i , 0.08 } , 1 b − 1 a , μ i + 2 ​ max ​ { s i , 0.08 } . \mu_{i}-2\max\{s_{i},0.08\},\qquad\frac{1}{b}-\frac{1}{a},\qquad\mu_{i}+2\max\{s_{i},0.08\}. We clip them to [ A i − , A i + ] [A_{i}^{-},A_{i}^{+}] and sort them. We hold the windows and reference moments fixed across models and throughout estimation; only the prior-mode cutpoint moves with a , b a,b . The integrand uses each model’s current likelihood and permanent-effect density. We apply L L -point Gauss–Legendre quadrature on each of the four subintervals, giving K α = 4 ​ L K_{\alpha}=4L nodes; zero-width intervals receive zero weight. We optimize with L = 16 L=16 ( K α = 64 K_{\alpha}=64 ) and report likelihoods with L = 32 L=32 ( K α = 128 K_{\alpha}=128 ). We assess these quadrature choices in the OU benchmark and at the empirical estimates in Appendix D.4 . Multiplying the quadrature weights by the common permanent-effect density gives w i ​ k ​ ( θ ) w_{ik}(\theta) in ( 4.8b ). We combine whole-history likelihoods by log-sum-exp. We compute scores by an exact reverse pass of the filter. This pass gives the derivatives of the log likelihood with respect to every transition probability, initial probability, grid node, transitory-shock parameter, and permanent-effect node. The maps from the parameters to the transition matrices, initial laws, and quadrature nodes and weights are cheap to evaluate, and we differentiate them by central differences. The PLV matrix exponential is the exception: we differentiate it by the adjoint of its Fréchet derivative, which costs about three matrix exponentials in total instead of two per parameter. For GMR, the tabulated loss kernels carry analytic derivatives. At cutpoint ties we follow the selected ordering branch and omit zero-width intervals. We optimize in transformed parameters: logarithms of positive parameters, logits of probabilities, and ρ = e − e η \rho=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{e}^{\eta}} for discrete-time persistence. We leave each mixture separation δ \delta in ( 4.2 ) unrestricted in sign. Swapping the component labels, ( p , δ , σ 1 , σ 2 ) ↦ ( 1 − p , − δ , σ 2 , σ 1 ) (p,\delta,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\mapsto(1-p,-\delta,\sigma_{2},\sigma_{1}) , leaves the distribution unchanged, so δ = 0 \delta=0 , the symmetric scale mixture, is an interior point. We relabel the estimates so that δ ≥ 0 \delta\geq 0 when we report them. We maximize with bounded L-BFGS-B, holding the grid fixed. Apart from the lower bounds on standard deviations described above, the bounds are wide and do not bind at the estimates. We stop when the projected gradient falls below 0.02 in the transformed parameters, or when five consecutive iterations together raise the log likelihood by less than 0.01. We use the second rule when progress becomes negligible. The quasi-Newton curvature serves only to guide optimization. We start OU with Gaussian transitory shocks at the exact estimate of specification (5) in Table 2 . We initialize GKOS and GMR with Gaussian transitory shocks near this estimate, perturbing the additional parameters away from the OU restrictions. For their versions with mixture transitory shocks, we combine each model’s Gaussian-specification estimates with the fitted OU transitory mixture. We initialize both PLV specifications from estimates on an earlier sample. We resume interrupted runs from saved parameter values.

sections.heading: D.4 Validation and numerical accuracy
sections.text: We validate both numerical transition constructions on OU, for which we can evaluate the likelihood exactly. This provides a known benchmark for the generator approach that we use for PLV. We include the Rouwenhorst (1995c) method for discretizing the Gaussian AR(1) process as an additional comparison. Specification (5) of Table 2 has a Gaussian OU state, Gaussian transitory noise, and the centered asymmetric-Laplace permanent effect. Appendix C derives its likelihood in closed form. We use the same 28,422 observations for 4,683 men as in § 3.1 . Write ℓ \ell for the exact log likelihood, θ ^ \widehat{\theta} for its maximizer, and ℓ N , K α \ell_{N,K_{\alpha}} for the HMM log likelihood. At θ ^ \widehat{\theta} , the estimates are κ ^ = 0.0797 \widehat{\kappa}=0.0797 , σ ^ = 0.2467 \widehat{\sigma}=0.2467 , σ ^ 0 = 0.2129 \widehat{\sigma}_{0}=0.2129 , σ ^ ϵ = 0.3145 \widehat{\sigma}_{\epsilon}=0.3145 , a ^ = 3.807 \widehat{a}=3.807 , and b ^ = 2.790 \widehat{b}=2.790 , so the stationary standard deviation of the state is ω = σ / 2 ​ κ = 0.618 \omega=\sigma/\sqrt{2\kappa}=0.618 .

sections.text: We first evaluate the numerical likelihood and its score at θ ^ \widehat{\theta} , holding the model and parameters fixed while we vary the numerical approximation. We re-estimate the parameters separately in Table 13 , then check numerical refinements at the empirical estimates in Table 15 . Because the exact score vanishes at θ ^ \widehat{\theta} , the numerical score s N ≔ ∇ ℓ N , K α ​ ( θ ^ ) s_{N}\coloneqq\nabla\ell_{N,K_{\alpha}}(\widehat{\theta}) measures how far the numerical estimator moves. Let H ≔ ∇ 2 ℓ ​ ( θ ^ ) H\coloneqq\nabla^{2}\ell(\widehat{\theta}) be the exact Hessian. To first order, the numerical estimator satisfies θ ^ N − θ ^ ≈ ( − H ) − 1 ​ s N \widehat{\theta}_{N}-\widehat{\theta}\approx(-H)^{-1}s_{N} , and the exact log likelihood loses 1 2 ​ s N ⊤ ​ ( − H ) − 1 ​ s N \frac{1}{2}s_{N}^{\top}(-H)^{-1}s_{N} . In the tables, SE denotes this reference scale from the observed information for the OU benchmark. We use it solely to express numerical parameter displacements. The signed error matters for model comparison, which uses likelihood levels. The implied bias matters for estimation, which uses likelihood slopes. We work in the transformed parameters of Appendix D.3 (logs of positive parameters); the ratios of numerical bias to these reference scales do not depend on this choice to first order. The re-estimation exercise also checks this first-order approximation.

sections.heading: Transition approximations at the exact estimate
sections.text: We compare the transition-density and generator constructions, with Rouwenhorst as a third benchmark. All three approximate the annual OU transition, which is the Gaussian AR(1) X t + 1 = ρ ​ X t + η t + 1 X_{t+1}=\rho X_{t}+\eta_{t+1} with ρ = e − κ \rho=\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa} and Var ⁡ ( η t + 1 ) = ω 2 ​ ( 1 − ρ 2 ) \var(\eta_{t+1})=\omega^{2}(1-\rho^{2}) . The method of Rouwenhorst (1995c) places N N evenly spaced nodes on [ − N − 1 ​ ω , N − 1 ​ ω ] [-\sqrt{N-1}\,\omega,\sqrt{N-1}\,\omega] . We use this same grid for the other two chains, so that at each N N the three chains differ only in their transition probabilities. The second chain is Farmer & Toda (2017g) , which matches the conditional mean and variance by relative entropy with Gaussian reference weights (Appendix D.1 ). The third chain is the diffusion generator of Appendix D.2 on a uniform generator grid with M = 4 ​ ( N − 1 ) + 1 M=4(N-1)+1 nodes, projected onto the filtering grid with composite Simpson weights. We take N = 2 k + 1 N=2^{k}+1 for k = 5 , … , 9 k=5,\dots,9 . All three chains reach an observation gap Δ \Delta through ( D.1 ). Timings are for one likelihood evaluation with our Python implementation on a 16-core laptop computer. Table 11 shows that the three chains behave very differently. The Farmer & Toda chain is accurate to 0.008 log points at N = 33 N=33 and exact to rounding from N = 65 N=65 . The Rouwenhorst chain overstates the log likelihood by 293 at N = 33 N=33 and still by 24 at N = 513 N=513 ; its error roughly halves when N N doubles. At N = 129 N=129 , a common choice, its score implies a bias of 5.1 standard errors in κ \kappa . The generator lies in between: its error falls from 55 to 1.7 and is below 0.4 standard errors from N = 129 N=129 . LL error is ℓ N , K α ​ ( θ ^ ) − ℓ ​ ( θ ^ ) \ell_{N,K_{\alpha}}(\widehat{\theta})-\ell(\widehat{\theta}) , where ℓ ⁡ ( θ ^ ) = − 22,595.35 \ell(\widehat{\theta})=-22{,}595.35 . Bias/SE is the largest implied first-order bias across the six parameters, in standard errors; for the Rouwenhorst chain and the generator, the largest bias is in κ \kappa . The generator uses M = 4 ​ ( N − 1 ) + 1 M=4(N-1)+1 nodes. Seconds are wall times for one likelihood evaluation and are similar across the three chains. Entries of 0.0000 are below 10 − 9 10^{-9} in absolute value. The differences come from how each chain approximates the conditional distribution. Farmer & Toda start from the Gaussian density at the nodes and adjust it only to match the first two conditional moments. For a smooth integrand, the resulting sums behave like the trapezoidal rule, which converges very fast once the spacing is below the conditional standard deviation (0.24 here). The Rouwenhorst chain counts how many of N − 1 N-1 two-state chains are in the high state. Starting from node i i , the next node is the sum of two independent binomials, Bin ⁡ ( i , p ) + Bin ⁡ ( N − 1 − i , 1 − p ) \mathrm{Bin}(i,p)+\mathrm{Bin}(N-1-i,1-p) with p = ( 1 + ρ ) / 2 p=(1+\rho)/2 . This distribution has full support and the exact conditional mean and variance, but it is skewed away from the center of the grid and has thinner tails than the Gaussian. It approaches the Gaussian only through the central limit theorem, which explains the slow convergence. The generator is a second-order approximation of the diffusion, so its error falls by a factor of four when the generator spacing halves. Two further features matter for applications. First, the nonzero errors reported in Table 11 are positive at this OU benchmark. A cruder discretization therefore gives a model a spurious likelihood advantage here, of 89 log points for the Rouwenhorst chain at N = 129 N=129 . The errors can have either sign at other parameters, as Table 14 shows. Second, the signed error and the implied bias measure different things. At N = 513 N=513 , the Rouwenhorst likelihood is 24 log points too high, but its implied loss from biased estimates is only 1.9; most of its error is a nearly constant shift. A constant shift is harmless for estimating one model but not for comparing models.

sections.heading: Re-estimation with numerical likelihoods
sections.text: We next re-estimate the OU model by maximizing ℓ N , K α \ell_{N,K_{\alpha}} and evaluate the exact likelihood at each numerical estimate (Table 13 ). For the Farmer & Toda chain, the numerical estimate coincides with θ ^ \widehat{\theta} . For the generator with N = 129 N=129 , the actual loss of 0.13 is close to the predicted 0.12, and each bias is within 0.02 standard errors of its first-order prediction. For the cubic grid, the actual and predicted losses are both 0.001, and the biases agree to within 0.001 standard errors. Thus the first-order approximation is reliable when the numerical likelihood is accurate. For the Rouwenhorst chain with N = 129 N=129 , the first-order approximation predicts an exact loss of 25 log points; the actual loss is 954. The numerical estimate has κ = 0.0093 \kappa=0.0093 instead of 0.0797, so the half-life of a persistent shock rises from 9 to 75 years, and σ ϵ \sigma_{\epsilon} falls from 0.31 to 0.24. Thus the Rouwenhorst likelihood has a spurious maximum far from θ ^ \widehat{\theta} . Lower κ \kappa widens the Rouwenhorst grid and coarsens its spacing, and lower σ ϵ \sigma_{\epsilon} makes the filter more sensitive to that spacing, so the optimizer moves toward parameters where the approximation overstates the likelihood the most. The following checks assess numerical sensitivity at the fitted parameters.

sections.heading: D.5 Implementation of the saving experiment
sections.text: This appendix gives the covariance transformations, earnings transitions, and household solution used in § 5 , followed by additional conditional results. The numerical checks below concern the fitted and covariance-matched processes under Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks.

sections.heading: Covariance matching
sections.text: The targets ( ρ , V , T ) (\rho,V,T) in ( 5.2 ) come from the fitted OU process. We use hats for the fitted parameters and stationary moments. For GKOS, we set persistence to ρ \rho and multiply the component means and standard deviations of its persistent innovation mixture by s η = ( 1 − ρ 2 ) ​ V / Var ^ ​ ( η ) s_{\eta}=\sqrt{(1-\rho^{2})V/\widehat{\var}(\eta)} . sections.heading: Earnings transitions
sections.text: We use N = 65 N=65 persistent states for the saving problem and compare N = 33 N=33 and 129 129 for the fitted and covariance-matched processes. Every model uses the same rule. The grid has N N evenly spaced nodes on ± N − 1 ​ V X , m \pm\sqrt{N-1}\sqrt{V_{X,m}} , where V X , m V_{X,m} is the model’s stationary persistent variance, and the transition probabilities match the conditional mean and variance of each row by the method of Farmer & Toda (2017g) . We use model-specific conditional moments and reference weights within this common rule. OU uses the Gaussian innovation density, GKOS the Gaussian-mixture innovation density, and GMR the Gaussian density of the state given each shared-loss node. For GMR, we retain the no-loss atom and integrate continuous log losses with 16-point Gauss–Laguerre quadrature, correcting its nodes to reproduce the exact first two loss moments. When the variance target lies outside the grid’s hull, a row matches only the mean, or keeps its reference weights if the mean also lies outside. This happens only in GMR rows with large losses. For PLV, the reference weights are the one-year transition probabilities of the generator of Appendix D.2 on 2,001 cubic-spaced nodes over [ − 40 , 40 ] [-40,40] , augmented by the coarse nodes, which we aggregate onto the coarse cells. The conditional variance comes from the same fine transition. A common spatial rescaling then corrects the stationary variance of the coarse chain without changing transition probabilities or the linear conditional mean; the factor lies between 0.990 and 1.008 at N = 65 N=65 . Across the fitted and covariance-matched cases and resolutions, the maximum discrepancy between numerical and analytical annual covariances, relative to the contemporaneous log-earnings variance, is below 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} , except for GMR with mixture shocks. There, rows with large losses leave discrepancies of up to 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} at N = 65 N=65 and 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} at N = 129 N=129 . We integrate independent transitory shocks using seven Gauss–Hermite nodes per Gaussian component. Let w m , j w_{m,j} denote the stationary probability of joint earnings outcome j j , including the shared loss where applicable, and let z m , j z_{m,j} denote its centered log earnings. We set y m , j = exp ⁡ ( z m , j ) ∑ k w m , k ​ exp ⁡ ( z m , k ) , Y m , j = y m , j + b . y_{m,j}=\frac{\exp(z_{m,j})}{\sum_{k}w_{m,k}\exp(z_{m,k})},\qquad Y_{m,j}=y_{m,j}+b. Thus mean raw earnings equal one at every numerical resolution, preserving transition probabilities and log covariances.

sections.heading: Household solution and numerical checks
sections.text: We solve consumption policies by the endogenous grid method ( Carroll, 2006c ) , using a 1,000-point exponential grid for saving on [ 0 , 10 6 ] [0,10^{6}] with median grid point 10, as in Ma & Toda (2022c) . Linear lotteries between adjacent asset nodes give the stationary joint distribution of assets and persistent states. For GMR, we integrate the lotteries and current utility using the joint law of the destination state, shared loss, and independent transitory shock. We draw the previous persistent state from stationarity before the first earnings transition to obtain the stationary current earnings law at zero initial assets. For the fitted and covariance-matched processes, at N = 65 N=65 , the 99th percentile of off-grid relative Euler residuals is below 0.003 % 0.003\% , and Bellman, budget, and asset-bound errors are below 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} . Truncating the saving grid at 10 5 10^{5} changes mean assets and CE by less than 10 − 14 10^{-14} in every case. Table 16 compares persistent-state resolutions under Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks. Changing N N from 65 to 129 changes mean assets by at most 0.7 % 0.7\% and CE by at most 0.3 % 0.3\% , except for fitted PLV, whose mean assets rise by 1.7 % 1.7\% because a wider grid captures more of its Pareto upper tail. N = 33 N=33 is adequate except for fitted PLV, whose mean assets are 2.7 % 2.7\% lower than at N = 65 N=65 . These changes are small relative to the differences across models. sections.heading: D.6 Calibration to moments of earnings changes and levels
sections.text: This appendix describes how we implement the calibration in § 5.2 . We fixed the targets, weights, and restrictions before running this calibration.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.text: Tables 18 – 20 list the 70 targets with their bootstrap standard errors and the calibrated model moments. A change belongs to the age group of its starting observation. The RE tercile of an observation is the tercile of its residual within its age group, and a change inherits the RE tercile of its starting observation. Guvenen et al. (2021g) rank workers by average earnings over the previous five years; our biennial short panel does not allow this average for most workers. For the mean subsequent changes in sets 3–4, we compute the deciles of the two-year change among the changes whose follow-up change over the given horizon exists. We do not target medians, which are close to zero in the residuals and make arc-percent deviations unstable. We also omit targets that our data or models cannot address. The mean earnings of lifetime-earnings groups in Guvenen et al. (2021g) require long histories, and their distribution of nonemployment requires the extensive margin. The slopes of the tails of the log density in Guvenen et al. (2026g) are too noisy with 22,619 two-year changes, and their cyclical moments have no counterpart in our stationary models.

sections.heading: Objective and parameters
sections.text: Following Guvenen et al. (2021g) , we minimize a weighted sum of squared arc-percent deviations, 2 ​ ( m k − d k ) / ( | m k | + | d k | ) 2(m_{k}-d_{k})/(\lvert m_{k}\rvert+\lvert d_{k}\rvert) , where m k m_{k} and d k d_{k} are the model and data values of moment k k . We assign weight 1 / 8 1/8 to each set and equal weights within sets. We calibrate the dynamic and transitory parameters together with σ 0 \sigma_{0} and ( a , b ) (a,b) : 9 parameters for OU, 11 for PLV, and 12 for GKOS and GMR.

sections.heading: Restrictions
sections.text: We keep the restrictions of Appendix D.7 : a lower bound of 0.025 on the standard deviations of transitory components, GKOS innovation components, and the GMR Gaussian innovation; ρ ≤ 0.99 \rho\leq 0.99 ; and, for PLV, 2 ​ κ / c + ≥ 1.1 2\kappa/c_{+}\geq 1.1 and 2 ​ κ / c − ≥ 0.4 2\kappa/c_{-}\geq 0.4 . We also restrict σ 0 ∈ [ 0.025 , 1.5 ] \sigma_{0}\in[0.025,1.5] and a , b ∈ [ 1.1 , 20 ] a,b\in[1.1,20] . These intervals contain the likelihood estimates by a wide margin.

sections.heading: Model moments
sections.text: We compute all model moments from simulated panels with the observed ages and observation gaps of all 4,683 men, as in § 4.4 , using the same formulas as in the data. Each simulated individual starts from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 0 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}) at age 30 and evolves annually through unobserved years. We hold all random draws fixed across parameter values. We draw each permanent effect by the inverse distribution function of the centered asymmetric Laplace law at a fixed uniform draw, so that the permanent effects move continuously with ( a , b ) (a,b) . OU, GKOS, and GMR evolve exactly at annual dates. For PLV, we simulate the finite-state chain whose annual transition matrix is exp ⁡ ( Q θ ) \exp(Q_{\theta}) , where Q θ Q_{\theta} is the generator of Appendix D.2 on cubic-spaced nodes over [ − 40 , 40 ] [-40,40] , as in Appendix D.5 . This matrix integrates over all movements within a year, so the simulation requires no time step. We draw each annual transition by inverting the cumulative probabilities of the current row at a fixed uniform draw. We use 501 nodes in the search, 1,001 nodes in the refinement, and 2,001 nodes for every reported objective. At the PLV likelihood estimate, at the PLV end point of Appendix D.7 , and at a stress point with c − = 0.83 c_{-}=0.83 , moments on 501 nodes differ from those on 2,001 nodes by at most 0.12, 0.17, and 0.48 bootstrap standard errors, respectively, and moments on 1,001 nodes by at most 0.19.

sections.heading: Search and evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate the objective at the likelihood estimate, at the end point of the calibration in Appendix D.7 (with σ 0 \sigma_{0} , a a , and b b at their likelihood estimates), and at 64 quasi-random points. We then run the Nelder–Mead method from the likelihood estimate, from that end point, and from the two best quasi-random points, with at most 3,000 evaluations each. The search uses 40 simulated panels. We refine the best end point with 100 panels and at most 500 evaluations. Optimizing over fixed draws can understate discrepancies from the targets. We therefore evaluate every reported objective on 200 new panels with draws independent of the search and refinement.

sections.heading: Alternative calibrations
sections.text: To set the tolerance in § 5.2 , we sum the squared ratios of the bootstrap standard errors to the absolute data moments, using the calibration weights. The sum is 0.0092. This first-order benchmark gives a scale for comparing objectives; it does not define a joint test of target fit. To construct the near-optimal ranges in Table 9 , we consider the end points of the four Nelder–Mead runs and nine search evaluations spread over persistence, whose search objectives are within 0.0092 of the search minimum. We re-evaluate their objectives on the new panels and retain candidates whose objectives are less than 0.0092 above that of the reported calibration. Candidates with lower objectives also qualify. The ranges cover the reported calibration and the retained candidates; they are neither confidence intervals nor exhaustive bounds over calibrations satisfying the tolerance. Tables 21 – 24 show the reported calibration, the four run end points, and the near-optimal candidates with the lowest and highest mean assets. Some runs stop far from the best objective, for example two of the four PLV runs.

sections.heading: D.7 Calibration to moments of earnings changes only
sections.text: We first calibrated each model to 18 moments of earnings changes only. We did this calibration first because it is computationally cheap: permanent effects cancel in changes, so the targets do not involve σ 0 \sigma_{0} , a a , or b b , and the moments of a discretized PLV process have closed forms. We then ran the calibration in § 5.2 to follow the designs of Guvenen et al. (2021g) and Guvenen et al. (2026g) more closely, including their moments of earnings levels. We report both calibrations. For each calibration, we fixed the targets and weights before computing its results. We added the parameter restrictions below after pilot runs of this calibration, for the reasons we give there.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.text: We adapt the one-, three-, and five-year horizons in the two papers to our biennial panel and target 18 moments of two-, four-, and six-year changes in the earnings residuals in ( 3.1 ). Table 25 groups the targets into five sets: two-year moments, six-year moments, the 10th and 90th percentiles, tail probabilities, and mean subsequent changes after extreme changes. Sets (i)–(ii) follow Guvenen et al. (2021g) , sets (iii)–(iv) follow Guvenen et al. (2026g) , and set (v) approximates the impulse responses in Guvenen et al. (2021g) . We start simulated histories from the age-30 law estimated by the HMM likelihood.

sections.heading: Objective and parameters
sections.text: The targets and their groups appear in Table 25 . Following Guvenen et al. (2021g) , we minimize a weighted sum of squared arc-percent deviations, 2 ​ ( m k − d k ) / ( | m k | + | d k | ) 2(m_{k}-d_{k})/(\lvert m_{k}\rvert+\lvert d_{k}\rvert) , where m k m_{k} and d k d_{k} are the model and data values of moment k k . We assign weight 1 / 5 1/5 to each set and equal weights within sets. Permanent effects cancel in changes, so the targets do not identify the permanent-effect rates ( a , b ) (a,b) . We retain their likelihood estimates in Table 4 . As a separate calibration choice, we also hold the initial dispersion σ 0 \sigma_{0} at its likelihood estimate. We calibrate the remaining dynamic and transitory parameters: 6 for OU, 8 for PLV, and 9 for GKOS and GMR.

sections.heading: Model moments
sections.text: For OU, GKOS, and GMR, we compute model moments from simulated panels with the observed ages and observation gaps of all 4,683 men, as in § 4.4 . Each simulated individual starts from the estimated Gaussian law at age 30 and evolves annually through unobserved years. We compute each moment using the same formulas as in the data. We use simulation because the coarse grids considered here poorly resolve persistent innovation components much narrower than the grid spacing. Such components arise in GKOS, whose innovation mixture can place one component near the lower bound of 0.025. For PLV, simulating the diffusion with fine time steps at every parameter value is costly, so we compute exact moments of a discretized process instead. We construct transitions from the fine generator as in Appendix D.5 . For calibration, the grid spans ± N − 1 \pm\sqrt{N-1} times the largest standard deviation of the state over ages 30–60. We propagate the estimated age-30 law through this chain. Each change is a finite mixture of Gaussian distributions. We evaluate its moments, tail probabilities, and conditional means using closed forms and find quantiles by numerically inverting the mixture distribution function. We pool pairs and triples with the observed counts by starting age. These moment calculations use the age schedules in the earnings data. For the saving experiment, we use each calibrated process’s stationary earnings law, as in § 5 .

sections.heading: Restrictions
sections.text: We impose a lower bound of 0.025 on transitory component standard deviations, GKOS innovation component standard deviations, and the GMR Gaussian innovation standard deviation. The bound matches the filtering grid spacing used for Table 4 and helps us evaluate the likelihood at the calibrated parameters accurately. We also restrict annual persistence to ρ ≤ 0.99 \rho\leq 0.99 and, for PLV, require 2 ​ κ / c + ≥ 1.1 2\kappa/c_{+}\geq 1.1 . These restrictions limit persistence and ensure that the stationary earnings distribution has a finite mean, with a Pareto upper-tail exponent of at least 1.1 for PLV. Without these restrictions, the pilot calibration pushes PLV toward a unit root ( ρ = 0.995 \rho=0.995 ) with an upper-tail exponent of 0.36. Stationary mean earnings are then infinite, which prevents the normalization to mean earnings of one used in § 5 . For PLV, we also require 2 ​ κ / c − ≥ 0.4 2\kappa/c_{-}\geq 0.4 . This bound regularizes extrapolation to the stationary lower tail beyond the observed ages 30–60. Without the bound, the calibrated exponent is 0.15, and the stationary standard deviation of the persistent state is 1.9. For context, the standard deviation of the observed log-earnings residual, which also includes permanent effects and transitory shocks, is 0.68–0.82 at ages 30–60. We set the bound below the likelihood estimate, 0.49, so that the restriction retains that estimate.

sections.heading: Search and evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate the objective at the likelihood estimate and at 50 quasi-random starting values. We then run the Nelder–Mead method from the likelihood estimate and from the three best of these values. For OU, GKOS, and GMR, we hold random draws fixed across parameter values, search with 40 simulated panels, and refine the best run end point with 100 panels. Optimizing over these draws can understate discrepancies from the targets. We therefore evaluate every reported objective for these models on 200 new panels with draws independent of the search and refinement. For PLV, we search with N = 129 N=129 nodes and refine the best point with N = 257 N=257 . 12 12 12 For PLV, the objective on 129 nodes differs from that on 257 nodes: at the best search point, it is 0.087 on 129 nodes and 0.065 on 257 nodes. The refinement on 257 nodes gives the reported calibration, but the near-optimal points for PLV come from the coarser search. We therefore re-evaluate them on 257 nodes. At the calibrated PLV parameters, 40 simulated panels with 100 time steps per year give an objective of 0.065, compared with 0.062 for the discretized process. We retain the refinement result as the reported calibration for each model and use the final evaluations to compare its objective with those of the other candidates.

sections.heading: Alternative calibrations
sections.text: To set the tolerance for this calibration, we sum the squared ratios of the bootstrap standard errors in Table 25 to the absolute data moments, using the calibration weights. The sum is approximately 0.006. This first-order benchmark gives a scale for comparing objectives; it does not define a joint test of target fit. To construct the near-optimal ranges in Table 26 , we consider the end points of the four Nelder–Mead runs and nine search evaluations spread over persistence, whose search objectives are within 0.006 of the search minimum. This screening uses the search criterion. We re-evaluate candidate objectives using the same procedure as for the reported calibration: independent simulation for OU, GKOS, and GMR, and the finer chain for PLV. We then retain candidates whose final objectives are less than 0.006 above the reported calibration’s final objective. Candidates with lower final objectives also qualify. The ranges cover the reported calibration and evaluated candidates with saving results; they are neither confidence intervals nor exhaustive bounds over calibrations satisfying the tolerance. Tables 27 – 30 show the reported calibration, the four run end points, and the near-optimal candidates with the lowest and highest mean assets.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Table 25 shows that calibration lowers the moment objective in every model. GKOS and GMR have the lowest calibrated objective values, 0.0010 and 0.0028, below the tolerance of 0.006. GKOS closely matches the standard deviation, skewness, and excess kurtosis of two-year changes. GMR closely matches skewness and excess kurtosis at the two- and six-year horizons. Both models also generate larger mean reversals after extreme losses than after extreme gains, as in the data. OU and PLV leave larger discrepancies. OU matches the excess kurtosis of two-year changes, but its symmetric changes prevent it from matching the skewness targets. Calibrated PLV produces excess kurtosis that rises between the two- and six-year horizons, whereas excess kurtosis falls in the data. The close fit to the targeted moments does not extend to earnings histories. Calibration lowers the log likelihood by 700 to 1,500 points relative to the likelihood estimates. Calibrated GKOS and GMR have log likelihoods of − 14,361 -14{,}361 and − 14,087 -14{,}087 , below every likelihood-estimated specification with mixture shocks in Table 4 . Table 26 reports saving and welfare. Calibrated GKOS and GMR imply mean assets of 18.1 and 13.2, more than twice their fitted values, and CE of 0.44 and 0.49, compared with 0.75 and 0.80. Among the near-optimal candidates, GKOS implies mean assets between 6.7 and 18.2, and GMR between 4.8 and 13.5. The reported GKOS and GMR calibrations have persistence near 0.99 and stationary persistent variances of about 1.5 (Tables 28 – 29 ). Moments of changes leave these features weakly determined. In § 5.2 , the moments of levels exclude such values: no near-optimal calibration of GKOS or GMR has a stationary persistent variance above 0.76. Both calibrations nevertheless lead to the same conclusions. Calibrations with close fit to their targets have log likelihoods below every likelihood-estimated specification with mixture shocks, and calibrations with similar target fit imply mean assets that differ by a factor of two or more. Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2611.02029v1 [econ.EM] 01 Nov 2026 \AtBeginRefsection \GenRefcontextData sorting=ynt \AtEveryCite \localrefcontext [sorting=ynt] Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk Jiuyi Cheng † † thanks: Emory University. Email: jiuyi.cheng@emory.edu . Alexis Akira Toda † † thanks: Department of Economics, Emory University and Research Institute for Economics and Business Administration, Kobe University. Email: alexis.akira.toda@emory.edu . Abstract Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined. Keywords: calibration, hidden Markov model, income risk, likelihood, misspecification, precautionary saving. JEL codes: C13, C52, C63, D15, E21. 1 Introduction Quantitative macroeconomics often disciplines models by calibration. A researcher chooses parameters so that the model reproduces a small set of selected moments of the data, and then uses the model to study behavior, welfare, or policy ( Kydland & Prescott, 1982c ; Kydland & Prescott, 1996c ) . 1 1 1 We use “calibration” to include procedures that fit a small set of selected moments, including the simulated method of moments as used in our application. Calibration is transparent and directs attention to features that the researcher considers important. However, agreement with the targets is evidence only about the targets. Different models, or different parameters within one model, may reproduce the same targets and still imply different responses to risk and policy ( Hansen & Heckman, 1996c ; Browning et al., 1999c ) . Whether this concern matters in practice is an empirical question: does matching the targets pin down the economic answer? Answering this question requires a criterion that uses more information than the selected moments. The likelihood is such a criterion. It evaluates the joint distribution of complete observed histories, so a model can reproduce selected statistics and still assign low probability to the histories from which we compute those statistics. The obstacle is computation. When a model contains a latent (unobserved) state with nonlinear dynamics or non-Gaussian shocks, the Kalman filter no longer applies, and the likelihood requires integrating over all possible paths of the latent state. Particle filters approximate this integral by simulation ( Fernández-Villaverde & Rubio-Ramírez, 2007c ) , but the simulated likelihood contains sampling noise and is not smooth in the parameters, which complicates optimization. For these reasons, likelihood comparison remains rare in quantitative work. In this paper, we show that maximum likelihood estimation of nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent-state models on short, irregular panels is now feasible, and that it leads to economic answers different from those of calibration. In our application, calibrations of a single earnings model fit the targets about equally well, yet imply mean assets that differ by a factor of about three, with the same data, preferences, and prices. The likelihood, by contrast, ranks the models and their parameters by their fit to complete earnings histories. We approximate the continuous latent state by a finite-state Markov chain while leaving the observations continuous. This approximation turns the model into a hidden Markov model (HMM), in which an unobserved finite-state chain generates the observed outcomes ( Kitagawa, 1987c ; Farmer, 2021g ) . For discrete-time processes, we construct the chain by the conditional moment matching method of Farmer & Toda (2017g) . For a diffusion, we discretize its generator (the operator that describes the local drift and variance of the diffusion). The HMM forward recursion sums over all latent histories by successive matrix multiplications. We integrate permanent individual effects (time-invariant unobserved differences) by numerical quadrature. We retain each individual’s entry age and use transition matrices for the actual observation gaps, so irregular observation dates pose no difficulty. The likelihood requires no simulation, and standard optimizers estimate all parameters jointly. We also provide a framework for inference and model comparison under misspecification. We treat each complete history as one independent observation and let the number of individuals grow while histories remain short. Under stated identification and regularity conditions, we give inference for the parameters and compare non-nested models using individual log likelihood differences ( White, 1982c ; Vuong, 1989c ) . The population likelihood ranks models by their Kullback–Leibler divergence (a measure of the discrepancy between two probability distributions) from the data distribution. We distinguish inference for the fixed finite-state approximation from inference for the continuous-state model, and we state conditions on the numerical approximation error. We apply the HMM approach to earnings dynamics, a central input into quantitative household models. We use 28,422 biennial observations of 4,683 men aged 30–60 from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), after removing deterministic earnings effects. We compare four processes for the persistent component of earnings. Our benchmark is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process, which is a Gaussian AR(1) at annual dates. The second is a stationary adaptation of Guvenen, Karahan, Ozkan & Song (2021g) (GKOS), an AR(1) whose innovations are a mixture of Gaussian distributions. The third is a stationary adaptation of Guvenen, McKay & Ryan (2026g) (GMR), an AR(1) with losses that affect both current earnings and the persistent state. The fourth is our piecewise linear variance (PLV) diffusion, whose volatility depends on the persistent state. Each process also includes permanent individual effects and either Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks, giving eight specifications. We show that all four stationary processes can share the entire earnings covariance function (Proposition 4.1 ). Thus second moments alone cannot separate them. Our application leads to three main results. First, the likelihood distinguishes the candidate specifications. Gaussian-mixture transitory shocks improve the log likelihood by more than 1,500 points in every model. Under this specification, PLV has the highest likelihood, followed by GKOS, GMR, and OU. The data favor PLV and GKOS over GMR but do not clearly separate PLV from GKOS. Second, close target fit need not extend to complete earnings histories. We calibrate each process with mixture transitory shocks to 70 moments of earnings changes and levels, following the designs of Guvenen et al. (2021g) ; Guvenen et al. (2026g) as closely as our data allow. To prevent cherry-picking, we fixed the targets and weights before computing any results. The calibrations match the percentiles of changes and levels closely and lower the moment objective by about 80 percent relative to the likelihood estimates. Yet all four calibrations fit the histories worse than every likelihood-estimated specification with mixture transitory shocks, including OU. 2 2 2 An earlier calibration to 18 moments of earnings changes only, in which GKOS and GMR match the targets within our tolerance, leads to the same conclusions (Appendix D.7 ). Third, the empirical criterion changes both the level of saving and the ranking of models. We solve a standard optimal saving problem, holding preferences, prices, mean earnings, and transfers fixed. When we match the processes to the fitted OU covariance function, PLV moves from the most wealth to the least, and mean assets fall within 4.2 to 4.8, compared with 4.8 to 10.5 under likelihood estimation. Calibrated PLV implies mean assets of 3.76, compared with 10.51 under likelihood estimation. Among evaluated calibrations whose objectives lie within 0.0092 of the reported objective, mean assets range from 2.2 to 8.2 for GKOS and from 3.1 to 9.3 for PLV. Thus close target fit can leave the economic answer largely undetermined. These results do not mean that the likelihood-preferred model is correct. Every model we consider is misspecified, and the fitted models still miss features of the data, including the extreme kurtosis of earnings changes. We therefore recommend a division of labor: use the likelihood to compare and select models, and use targeted moments to diagnose where the selected model fails. The HMM approach applies whenever the latent state is low-dimensional, so researchers can assess the fit of observed histories before using a model for economic analysis. In empirical industrial organization, researchers routinely estimate and test structural models by likelihood ( Rust, 1987c ) . The HMM approach makes the same discipline available for the household models of quantitative macroeconomics. 1.1 Related literature Our paper contributes to the literature on the empirical foundations of quantitative models. Kydland & Prescott (1982c) ; Kydland & Prescott (1996c) develop and defend calibration as a computational experiment. Hansen & Heckman (1996c) and Browning et al. (1999c) examine the empirical support for the parameters and specifications used in quantitative macroeconomics. Gregory & Smith (1991c) and Canova (1994c) develop simulation-based inference for calibrated models, and Watson (1993c) measures discrepancies in their dynamic second moments. Hnatkovska et al. (2012c) compare misspecified calibrated models by minimum distance and study the role of the weighting matrix. Andrews et al. (2017c) measure the local sensitivity of parameter estimates to estimation moments. Closely related to our application, Crawley et al. (2026c) show that misspecification makes income-risk estimates depend on the moments and weights used, and they propose a richer transitory component. We instead compare models by the likelihood of complete observed histories and show that close target fit can leave economic predictions undetermined. The HMM approximation of continuous-state models has a long history. Kitagawa (1987c) evaluates non-Gaussian state-space likelihoods by numerical integration, and Langrock et al. (2012c) maximize the likelihood of fine-grid HMM approximations to nonlinear models. Farmer (2021g) develops the “discretization filter” for economic models, combines HMM likelihood evaluation with moment-matching discretizations such as Farmer & Toda (2017g) , and establishes likelihood theory for long time series. Altman (2007c) develops mixed HMMs with random effects, and Delattre et al. (2013c) study likelihood estimation of diffusions with random effects. We bring HMM likelihood evaluation and comparison into a short-panel framework with permanent heterogeneity, nonstationary initialization, and irregular observation gaps. We give inference under misspecification and separate the statistical conditions from the conditions on numerical accuracy. Our illustration builds on the earnings-dynamics literature. Abowd & Card (1989c) and Meghir & Pistaferri (2011c) study the covariance structure of earnings, and Storesletten et al. (2004c) use earnings risk in a quantitative household model. Geweke & Keane (2000c) estimate PSID earnings dynamics with normal-mixture shocks by Bayesian methods. Meghir & Pistaferri (2004c) and Botosaru & Sasaki (2018c) allow state-dependent variances, and Arellano et al. (2017c) allow nonlinear persistence. Guvenen et al. (2021g) document non-Gaussian earnings changes in administrative data, and Guvenen et al. (2026g) propose a tractable process with large losses and scarring. De et al. (2020c) and Guvenen et al. (2024c) study the consumption and welfare implications of richer earnings risk. We use earnings dynamics to demonstrate HMM model selection and measure how the choice of empirical criterion changes economic predictions. 2 Hidden Markov likelihood for short panels In this section, we describe how we evaluate and compare likelihoods of short-panel models. We approximate the continuous latent state by a finite-state Markov chain, which turns the model into a hidden Markov model (HMM). We let the number of independent individuals grow while individual histories remain bounded in length. Our inference accommodates permanent heterogeneity without requiring the latent process to mix over time. We use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) because it is widely used and readily available, allowing readers to reproduce the exercise without access to restricted administrative records. We compare models for reported earnings, which include survey noise. We describe the data and estimate a benchmark with Gaussian persistent and transitory shocks by exact maximum likelihood. We examine how permanent heterogeneity and initial dispersion affect the estimates. 3.1 Data and deterministic adjustment We use 14 biennial PSID interviews from 1997 through 2023, which report annual labor earnings for income years 1996, 1998, …, 2022. We follow individuals using their 1968 family identifier and person number, selecting annual labor earnings for their current role as Reference Person or spouse/partner. We compute each individual’s birth year as the rounded median of interview year minus reported age. We use this birth year to define income-year age and measure elapsed time from age 30. The baseline sample contains men ages 30–60 in the income year who are current Reference Persons, spouses, or partners. We require positive, nonmissing annual labor earnings and nonmissing completed education, as well as at least two usable observations per person, but not a balanced panel. We keep only the SRC core sample (1968 family identifiers 1–2,930). This restriction drops the Census low-income oversample and the immigrant samples added from 1997, so that the unweighted sample does not overrepresent low-income households. Following Guvenen et al. (2021g) , we also require annual labor earnings of at least 13 weeks of 40 hours at half the federal minimum wage ( $ 1,885 \$1{,}885 for income years 2010–2022), which excludes observations with minimal attachment to the labor market.
